text: How clearly doth it appear unto thee, that no other course of thy life could fit a true philosopher's practice better, than this very course, that thou art now already in?
plain: Where you already live may suit steady practice far better than some imagined cleaner path. Work, family, and the present routine are enough material for living with care.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: A branch cut off from the continuity of that which was next unto it, must needs be cut off from the whole tree: so a man that is divided from another man, is divided from the whole society.
plain: Twigs broken away from the neighbour branch are broken away from the whole tree. Pulling back from one person can, in the same manner, separate you from the wider group.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: To grow together like fellow branches in matter of good correspondence and affection; but not in matter of opinions.
plain: Grow close to people in warmth and fair dealing, the way neighbouring branches share a tree. You do not have to share every opinion to stay properly connected.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: It is not possible that any nature should be inferior unto art, since that all arts imitate nature.
plain: No natural thing sits below human craft, because every craft copies what nature already does. A well made tool or meal still follows patterns older than the workshop.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Whatsoever thou doest hereafter aspire unto, thou mayest even now enjoy and possess, if thou doest not envy thyself thine own happiness.
plain: Hopes for a later feeling can be yours now, if you stop standing in the way of your own contentment. The missing piece is often permission, not a different life.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: How ridiculous and strange is he, that wonders at anything that happens in this life in the ordinary course of nature!
plain: Astonishment at the ordinary run of things is a strange habit to keep. Illness, delay, and change at home are usual events, however sharply they happen to land.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Either fate, (and that either an absolute necessity, and unavoidable decree; or a placable and flexible Providence) or all is a mere casual confusion, void of all order and government.
plain: Events are either arranged, whether fixed hard or able to bend, or they are a muddle with no order at all. Living as if some order holds is the steadier bet.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: At the conceit and apprehension that such and such a one hath sinned, thus reason with thyself; What do I know whether this be a sin indeed, as it seems to be?
plain: Seeming plainly in the wrong may only be how it looks from your seat. A colleague may have reasons you have not heard yet, so hold the verdict.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: If it be not fitting, do it not. If it be not true, speak it not. Ever maintain thine own purpose and resolution free from all compulsion and necessity.
plain: Leave undone what does not fit, and leave unsaid what is not true. Keep your aim free enough that neither pressure at work nor habit at home is dragging it.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Of everything that presents itself unto thee, to consider what the true nature of it is, and to unfold it, as it were, by dividing it into that which is formal: that which is material: the true use or end of it, and the just time that it is appointed to last.
plain: Unpack whatever shows up into what it is, what it is made of, what it is for, and how long it should last. A worry or a purchase grows clearer that way.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: It is high time for thee, to understand that there is somewhat in thee, better and more divine than either thy passions, or thy sensual appetites and affections.
plain: There is something in you steadier than moods and bodily cravings, and it is time to notice it. That part can guide an evening when appetite, anger, or habit starts to steer.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Remember that all is but opinion, and all opinion depends of the mind. Take thine opinion away, and then as a ship that hath stricken in within the arms and mouth of the harbour, a present calm; all things safe and steady: a bay, not capable of any storms and tempests: as the poet hath it.
plain: Much of what shakes you is the view your mind adds, and that view can be set down. Without it, the day sits quiet, like a boat that has reached shelter.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: No operation whatsoever it he, ceasing for a while, can be truly said to suffer any evil, because it is at an end.
plain: An activity that stops has not been harmed just because it has finished. A job, a conversation, or a season of life can end without that ending being an injury.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: These three things thou must have always in a readiness: first concerning thine own actions, whether thou doest nothing either idly, or otherwise, than justice and equity do require: and concerning those things that happen unto thee externally, that either they happen unto thee by chance, or by providence; of which two to accuse either, is equally against reason.
plain: Three checks belong in ordinary life. Your actions should be neither pointless nor unfair, outside events arrive by chance or by some order, and blaming either one goes against good sense.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Cast away from thee opinion, and thou art safe. And what is it that hinders thee from casting of it away?
plain: Set the extra opinion down and the situation feels safer than it did. Very little stops you from doing that, apart from the habit of gripping a view you could loosen.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: God beholds our minds and understandings, bare and naked from these material vessels, and outsides, and all earthly dross.
plain: Bare of clothes, job title, and other outer wrapping, a person is much easier to see truly. The mind stands clearer once that earthly clutter is set aside.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Let thy thoughts ever run upon them, who once for some one thing or other, were moved with extraordinary indignation; who were once in the highest pitch of either honour, or calamity; or mutual hatred and enmity; or of any other fortune or condition whatsoever.
plain: Think of people once furious, once high in honour or deep in trouble, or locked in mutual dislike. Those peaks were real, and they passed out of the day they filled.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: To them that ask thee, Where hast thou seen the Gods, or how knowest thou certainly that there be Gods, that thou art so devout in their worship?
plain: Asked where you have seen the order that makes your respect so steady, you can answer without a show. Modest and firm is enough for that question from a friend.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Herein doth consist happiness of life, for a man to know thoroughly the true nature of everything; what is the matter, and what is the form of it: with all his heart and soul, ever to do that which is just, and to speak the truth. What then remaineth but to enjoy thy life in a course and coherence of good actions, one upon another immediately succeeding, and never interrupted, though for never so little a while?
plain: Contentment lies in seeing what things really are, acting fairly with your whole heart, and speaking truthfully. After that, enjoy a steady run of decent actions with scarcely a gap.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: There is but one light of the sun, though it be intercepted by walls and mountains, and other thousand objects.
plain: One daylight remains, even when walls, hills, and countless objects stand in the way. A clear mind can be blocked by work or noise and still be the same light.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: What doest thou desire? To live long. What? To enjoy the operations of a sensitive soul; or of the appetitive faculty? or wouldst thou grow, and then decrease again?
plain: Wanting a very long life deserves a closer look at what you are actually after. More sensation, more appetite, or time to grow and then fade is a thin prize.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: What a small portion of vast and infinite eternity it is, that is allowed unto every one of us, and how soon it vanisheth into the general age of the world: of the common substance, and of the common soul also what a small portion is allotted unto us: and in what a little clod of the whole earth (as it were) it is that thou doest crawl.
plain: Each of us gets a tiny slice of the long span, and it fades quickly. Our share of the whole is small, and we move about on one little patch of ground.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: What is the present estate of my understanding? For herein lieth all indeed. As for all other things, they are without the compass of mine own will: and if without the compass of my will, then are they as dead things unto me, and as it were mere smoke.
plain: Ask what state your understanding is in right now, because that is the part that counts. Everything outside your choice is, for you, like smoke, unable to steer the next hour.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: To stir up a man to the contempt of death this among other things, is of good power and efficacy, that even they who esteemed pleasure to be happiness, and pain misery, did nevertheless many of them contemn death as much as any.
plain: Even people who treated pleasure as the whole point, and pain as the only misery, often faced death with little fuss. Comfort is not the only source of nerve.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: I have often wondered how it should come to pass, that every man loving himself best, should more regard other men's opinions concerning himself than his own.
plain: People who care about themselves most still rate other people's views of them above their own, which is a strange reversal. A comment online can outweigh the judgement you already trust.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: how come it to pass that the Gods having ordered all other things so well and so lovingly, should be overseen in this one only thing, that whereas then hath been some very good men that have made many covenants as it were with God and by many holy actions and outward services contracted a kind of familiarity with Him; that these men when once they are dead, should never be restored to life, but be extinct for ever.
plain: It can seem uneven that so much is carefully arranged, while decent people who lived close to what they revered simply end. The puzzle still meets anyone watching a good life close.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Use thyself even unto those things that thou doest at first despair of. For the left hand we see, which for the most part lieth idle because not used; yet doth it hold the bridle with more strength than the right, because it hath been used unto it.
plain: Practise tasks you first think are beyond you. A little-used hand can hold the reins more firmly than the busy one, once use has trained it, and work skills grow that way.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: All worldly things thou must behold and consider, dividing them into matter, form, and reference, or their proper end.
plain: Ordinary things get clearer split into what they are made of, the shape they take, and the purpose they serve. A phone, a meal, or a quarrel simplifies in those three parts.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: How happy is man in this his power that hath been granted unto him: that he needs not do anything but what God shall approve, and that he may embrace contentedly, whatsoever God doth send unto him?
plain: Freedom, in this sense, is doing only what you could stand to have seen, and taking what arrives without a fight. That pair of powers is available on a very ordinary day.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Whatsoever doth happen in the ordinary course and consequence of natural events, neither the Gods, (for it is not possible, that they either wittingly or unwittingly should do anything amiss) nor men, (for it is through ignorance, and therefore against their wills that they do anything amiss) must be accused. None then must be accused.
plain: For what follows the ordinary run of events, there is nobody useful to blame. People slip through not knowing, and the wider order is not plotting a personal injury against you.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Remember how long thou hast already put off these things, and how often a certain day and hour as it were, having been set unto thee by the gods, thou hast neglected it.
plain: Remember how long you have postponed the changes you meant to make, and how many set moments you let slide. Another evening will not be kinder just because you waited.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Consider with thyself how man, and by what part of his, is joined unto God, and how that part of man is affected, when it is said to be diffused.
plain: Consider which part of you joins something larger than your moods, and what happens when that part scatters. Spread thin across the phone and the day, it stops its proper work.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: If thou shouldst live three thousand, or as many as ten thousands of years, yet remember this, that man can part with no life properly, save with that little part of life, which he now lives: and that which he lives, is no other, than that which at every instant he parts with.
plain: Thousands of years would leave you living only this small present stretch, and letting go of it moment by moment. A long span would still arrive one ordinary hour at a time.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Remember that all is but opinion and conceit, for those things are plain and apparent, which were spoken unto Monimus the Cynic; and as plain and apparent is the use that may be made of those things, if that which is true and serious in them, be received as well as that which is sweet and pleasing.
plain: Life is largely opinion, and that old line is useful once you keep its serious side with the pleasing one. How you read a slight or a win does half the work.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: A man's soul doth wrong and disrespect itself first and especially, when as much as in itself lies it becomes an aposteme, and as it were an excrescency of the world, for to be grieved and displeased with anything that happens in the world, is direct apostacy from the nature of the universe; part of which, all particular natures of the world, are.
plain: Minds wrong themselves when they turn into a sore spot on the world, upset by whatever happens. That sulk cuts you off from the larger order your life already belongs to.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: The time of a man's life is as a point; the substance of it ever flowing, the sense obscure; and the whole composition of the body tending to corruption.
plain: Our time alive is a pinpoint, its stuff moving, its grasp hazy, and the body on the way to wearing out. Held lightly, that view loosens your grip on a single week.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Let it be thy earnest and incessant care as a Roman and a man to perform whatsoever it is that thou art about, with true and unfeigned gravity, natural affection, freedom and justice: and as for all other cares, and imaginations, how thou mayest ease thy mind of them.
plain: Give the task in front of you real weight, natural warmth, freedom, and fairness, and set the other worries down. That is enough dignity for a working day, without the extra theatre.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Do, soul, do; abuse and contemn thyself; yet a while and the time for thee to respect thyself, will be at an end. Every man's happiness depends from himself, but behold thy life is almost at an end, whiles affording thyself no respect, thou dost make thy happiness to consist in the souls, and conceits of other men.
plain: Slighting your own mind can continue, but the time left for treating it properly is short. Contentment depends on you, yet it leaks away while you lodge it in other people's opinions.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Why should any of these things that happen externally, so much distract thee? Give thyself leisure to learn some good thing, and cease roving and wandering to and fro.
plain: Outside events do not deserve this much of your attention. Leave yourself time to learn one useful thing, and stop drifting from tab to tab and task to task.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: These things thou must always have in mind: What is the nature of the universe, and what is mine--in particular: This unto that what relation it hath: what kind of part, of what kind of universe it is: And that there is nobody that can hinder thee, but that thou mayest always both do and speak those things which are agreeable to that nature, whereof thou art a part.
plain: Hold in view the wider order and your own nature, and how the second sits inside the first. Nobody can stop you speaking and acting in a way that fits that place.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Theophrastus, where he compares sin with sin (as after a vulgar sense such things I grant may be compared:) says well and like a philosopher, that those sins are greater which are committed through lust, than those which are committed through anger.
plain: Faults that come from chasing pleasure sit heavier than faults that come from a flash of anger. Wanting the next treat, drink, or comfort is a choice anger often is not.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Whatsoever thou dost affect, whatsoever thou dost project, so do, and so project all, as one who, for aught thou knowest, may at this very present depart out of this life.
plain: Do the task, and make the plan, as someone who might have to leave today. That stance tidies priorities at work and at home faster than a long list of hopes.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Consider how quickly all things are dissolved and resolved: the bodies and substances themselves, into the matter and substance of the world: and their memories into the general age and time of the world.
plain: Things come apart quickly, bodies back into the world's stuff and memories into the long stretch of time. A reputation or a quarrel has a shorter life than it feels today.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: A man must not only consider how daily his life wasteth and decreaseth, but this also, that if he live long, he cannot be certain, whether his understanding shall continue so able and sufficient, for either discreet consideration, in matter of businesses; or for contemplation: it being the thing, whereon true knowledge of things both divine and human, doth depend.
plain: Life thins a little every day, and a long span does not guarantee a mind still fit for careful work or quiet thought. Use your understanding while it is still sharp.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Use thine opinative faculty with all honour and respect, for in her indeed is all: that thy opinion do not beget in thy understanding anything contrary to either nature, or the proper constitution of a rational creature.
plain: Treat your power of judgement with real respect, because so much depends on it. Do not let an opinion grow that fights your nature or the make-up of a thinking person.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: What is this, that now my fancy is set upon? of what things doth it consist? how long can it last? which of all the virtues is the proper virtue for this present use? as whether meekness, fortitude, truth, faith, sincerity, contentation, or any of the rest?
plain: Name what your mind has fixed on, what it is made of, and how long it can last. Then pick the fitting strength, whether patience, courage, honesty, or simple contentment.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: As physicians and chirurgeons have always their instruments ready at hand for all sudden cures; so have thou always thy dogmata in a readiness for the knowledge of things, both divine and human: and whatsoever thou dost, even in the smallest things that thou dost, thou must ever remember that mutual relation, and connection that is between these two things divine, and things human.
plain: Have your working principles as ready as a doctor keeps tools, for questions both large and human. Even in small tasks, remember how the wide order and daily life are tied together.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Be not deceived; for thou shalt never live to read thy moral commentaries, nor the acts of the famous Romans and Grecians; nor those excerpta from several books; all which thou hadst provided and laid up for thyself against thine old age. Hasten therefore to an end, and giving over all vain hopes, help thyself in time if thou carest for thyself, as thou oughtest to do.
plain: Notes and books saved for later years are unlikely to be reached. Drop that idle hope and help your own mind now, while the care can still change today.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: To steal, to sow, to buy, to be at rest, to see what is to be done (which is not seen by the eyes, but by another kind of sight:) what these words mean, and how many ways to be understood, they do not understand. The body, the soul, the understanding. As the senses naturally belong to the body, and the desires and affections to the soul, so do the dogmata to the understanding.
plain: Body, feeling, and judging mind get mixed up, and so ordinary acts like buying, resting, or seeing what should be done are misread. Senses, impulses, and principles are not the same layer.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: To be capable of fancies and imaginations, is common to man and beast. To be violently drawn and moved by the lusts and desires of the soul, is proper to wild beasts and monsters, such as Phalaris and Nero were.
plain: Picturing things is common to people and animals, but being hauled about by craving belongs with the wild and the cruel. You can notice a want without letting it drag the evening.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Hippocrates having cured many sicknesses, fell sick himself and died. The Chaldeans and Astrologians having foretold the deaths of divers, were afterwards themselves surprised by the fates.
plain: Doctors who healed many others still sickened and died, and people who predicted deaths were caught out by their own. Skill and forecasts do not lift anyone out of the common ending.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Spend not the remnant of thy days in thoughts and fancies concerning other men, when it is not in relation to some common good, when by it thou art hindered from some other better work.
plain: Days left to you are poorly spent turning over other people's business, unless it serves some shared good. That habit blocks better work waiting on your own list.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Do nothing against thy will, nor contrary to the community, nor without due examination, nor with reluctancy.
plain: Act with your will behind it, alongside other people, after a proper look, and with no inner drag. A resentful yes at home or at work is a poor action.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: To be cheerful, and to stand in no need, either of other men's help or attendance, or of that rest and tranquillity, which thou must be beholding to others for. Rather like one that is straight of himself, or hath ever been straight, than one that hath been rectified.
plain: Be cheerful with no need for other people to prop you up or to supply your calm. Better to have grown straight on your own than to need straightening later.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Never esteem of anything as profitable, which shall ever constrain thee either to break thy faith, or to lose thy modesty; to hate any man, to suspect, to curse, to dissemble, to lust after anything, that requireth the secret of walls or veils.
plain: Call nothing a gain if it makes you break your word, drop your modesty, hate, suspect, pretend, or chase a hidden pleasure. A want that needs closed doors costs too much.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: In the mind that is once truly disciplined and purged, thou canst not find anything, either foul or impure, or as it were festered: nothing that is either servile, or affected: no partial tie; no malicious averseness; nothing obnoxious; nothing concealed.
plain: Once cleared properly, the mind holds nothing rotten, cringing, or put on for show. No secret grudge, no sly loyalty, and nothing tucked away that you would hate to have seen.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: That inward mistress part of man if it be in its own true natural temper, is towards all worldly chances and events ever so disposed and affected, that it will easily turn and apply itself to that which may be, and is within its own power to compass, when that cannot be which at first it intended.
plain: Judgement in good shape bends to what it can still do once the first plan fails. A cancelled meeting then becomes the next right task rather than a collapse.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: These two rules, thou must have always in a readiness. First, do nothing at all, but what reason proceeding from that regal and supreme part, shall for the good and benefit of men, suggest unto thee.
plain: Firm rules belong within reach. Do nothing except what your best judgement suggests for the good of other people, whether that shows up at work, at home, or in a small favour.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Hast thou reason? I have. Why then makest thou not use of it? For if thy reason do her part, what more canst thou require?
plain: Reason is already yours, so the live question is whether you actually use it today. If that power does its work, little else is required for the next decision at hand.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: As a part hitherto thou hast had a particular subsistence: and now shalt thou vanish away into the common substance of Him, who first begot thee, or rather thou shalt be resumed again into that original rational substance, out of which all others have issued, and are propagated. Many small pieces of frankincense are set upon the same altar, one drops first and is consumed, another after; and it comes all to one.
plain: Your stretch as one distinct part ends when you fold back into the larger whole. Some finish sooner and some later, like incense grains, and it comes to the same thing.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Within ten days, if so happen, thou shalt be esteemed a god of them, who now if thou shalt return to the dogmata and to the honouring of reason, will esteem of thee no better than of a mere brute, and of an ape.
plain: Crowds that praise you to the skies within a fortnight will call you dull if you stick to good sense. Chasing that swing of opinion is a poor use of a week.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Not as though thou hadst thousands of years to live. Death hangs over thee: whilst yet thou livest, whilst thou mayest, be good.
plain: Thousands of years are not waiting for you, and the end is already near enough to matter. While you are here and still able, spend the time being decent.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Now much time and leisure doth he gain, who is not curious to know what his neighbour hath said, or hath done, or hath attempted, but only what he doth himself, that it may be just and holy? or to express it in Agathos' words, Not to look about upon the evil conditions of others, but to run on straight in the line, without any loose and extravagant agitation.
plain: Hours come back when you ignore what a neighbour said or tried, and watch only whether your own action is fair. Keep on your line instead of scanning other people's faults.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: He who is greedy of credit and reputation after his death, doth not consider, that they themselves by whom he is remembered, shall soon after every one of them be dead; and they likewise that succeed those; until at last all memory, which hitherto by the succession of men admiring and soon after dying hath had its course, be quite extinct.
plain: Hunger for a name after you are gone forgets that the people who remember you will die too, and so will the next lot. Memory thins until that praise is almost gone.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: If so be that the souls remain after death (say they that will not believe it); how is the air from all eternity able to contain them?
plain: Supposing minds went on after death, some ask how the air could have held them through endless time. Clever as that objection is, it does not decide how to live this week.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Not to wander out of the way, but upon every motion and desire, to perform that which is just: and ever to be careful to attain to the true natural apprehension of every fancy, that presents itself.
plain: Stay on the path, and at each urge do the fair thing, seeing the impression clearly before you chase it. That simple habit keeps an evening from wandering off into noise.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Whatsoever is expedient unto thee, O World, is expedient unto me; nothing can either be 'unseasonable unto me, or out of date, which unto thee is seasonable.
plain: Whatever fits the wider world can fit you, including the timing. If the season is right for the whole, it is not late or early merely because it jars with your plan.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Let nothing be done rashly, and at random, but all things according to the most exact and perfect rules of art.
plain: Rash, random action wastes the craft you could bring to a job. Even small tasks at home go better when the result is chosen with care rather than left to accident.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: They will say commonly, Meddle not with many things, if thou wilt live cheerfully.
plain: Cheerful living, people often say, means refusing to meddle in too many things. There is sense in that, when every extra commitment steals quiet from the evening you meant to keep.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Try also how a good man's life; (of one, who is well pleased with those things whatsoever, which among the common changes and chances of this world fall to his own lot and share; and can live well contented and fully satisfied in the justice of his own proper present action, and in the goodness of his disposition for the future:) will agree with thee.
plain: Test this pattern and see if it suits you. Be pleased with the share that lands, content with a fair action today, and well disposed for whatever comes next at work.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Either this world is a κόσμος or comely piece, because all disposed and governed by certain order: or if it be a mixture, though confused, yet still it is a comely piece.
plain: Either the world is ordered and therefore a fitting whole, or it is a muddle and still somehow fitting. The scene you live and work in is not mere rubbish either way.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: A black or malign disposition, an effeminate disposition; an hard inexorable disposition, a wild inhuman disposition, a sheepish disposition, a childish disposition; a blockish, a false, a scurril, a fraudulent, a tyrannical: what then? If he be a stranger in the world, that knows not the things that are in it; why not be a stranger as well, that wonders at the things that are done in it?
plain: Sour, timid, childish, false, or bullying tempers all miss the mark, and so does gaping at everyday events. Amazement at events is its own way of being a stranger here.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: He is a true fugitive, that flies from reason, by which men are sociable. He blind, who cannot see with the eyes of his understanding.
plain: Real runaways flee good sense, the very thing that lets people live together. Blindness is failing to look with the mind, however sharp the eyes happen to be.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: There is, who without so much as a coat; and there is, who without so much as a book, doth put philosophy in practice. I am half naked, neither have I bread to eat, and yet I depart not from reason, saith one. But I say; I want the food of good teaching, and instructions, and yet I depart not from reason.
plain: Some live by good sense with no coat and no book, and some go hungry and still stay with it. You can lack lessons and still refuse to leave reason behind.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: What art and profession soever thou hast learned, endeavour to affect it, and comfort thyself in it; and pass the remainder of thy life as one who from his whole heart commits himself and whatsoever belongs unto him, unto the gods: and as for men, carry not thyself either tyrannically or servilely towards any.
plain: Stay with the craft you learned and let it steady the years that remain. With others be neither a bully nor a doormat, and loosen your grip on cares you cannot hold.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Those words which once were common and ordinary, are now become obscure and obsolete; and so the names of men once commonly known and famous, are now become in a manner obscure and obsolete names.
plain: Words everyone once used now sound strange, and names that were famous have faded the same way. Today's slogans and well known people are on that path, however loud they seem.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Whatsoever is now present, and from day to day hath its existence; all objects of memories, and the minds and memories themselves, incessantly consider, all things that are, have their being by change and alteration.
plain: Look steadily at what is here today, at the things you remember, and at memory itself. All of it exists by changing, including the plans and faces you expect to stay put.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: They seek for themselves private retiring places, as country villages, the sea-shore, mountains; yea thou thyself art wont to long much after such places.
plain: Quiet retreats in a village, on a shore, or up a hill are widely longed for, and you have wanted that too. The mind's noise often travels along with the bags.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Thou art now ready to die, and yet hast thou not attained to that perfect simplicity: thou art yet subject to many troubles and perturbations; not yet free from all fear and suspicion of external accidents; nor yet either so meekly disposed towards all men, as thou shouldest; or so affected as one, whose only study and only wisdom is, to be just in all his actions.
plain: Near the end, you may still lack simplicity, still fear outside mishaps, and still fall short of a kind, fair aim. Some of that gap can be closed while you are here.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Behold and observe, what is the state of their rational part; and those that the world doth account wise, see what things they fly and are afraid of; and what things they hunt after.
plain: Watch the state of people's judgement, especially those called wise, and notice what they run from and what they chase. Fear and appetite in the admired are a useful lesson.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: In another man's mind and understanding thy evil Cannot subsist, nor in any proper temper or distemper of the natural constitution of thy body, which is but as it were the coat or cottage of thy soul.
plain: Harm does not live inside someone else's mind, nor in the body's passing aches, which are more like a coat you wear. The disturbance that matters sits closer than either of those.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Ever consider and think upon the world as being but one living substance, and having but one soul, and how all things in the world, are terminated into one sensitive power; and are done by one general motion as it were, and deliberation of that one soul; and how all things that are, concur in the cause of one another's being, and by what manner of connection and concatenation all things happen.
plain: Picture the world as one living thing with one life running through it, so events share a single movement. What happens to you is tied to what happens elsewhere, far from home.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: What art thou, that better and divine part excepted, but as Epictetus said well, a wretched soul, appointed to carry a carcass up and down?
plain: Set aside the better part of you, and what remains is a mind hauling a body from place to place. Remembering that can shrink vanity about looks, clothes, and health.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: To suffer change can be no hurt; as no benefit it is, by change to attain to being. The age and time of the world is as it were a flood and swift current, consisting of the things that are brought to pass in the world. For as soon as anything hath appeared, and is passed away, another succeeds, and that also will presently out of sight.
plain: Changing is not a harm, any more than arriving by change was a special prize, and life is a fast current where one thing appears and the next slips out of sight.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Whatsoever doth happen in the world, is, in the course of nature, as usual and ordinary as a rose in the spring, and fruit in summer.
plain: Events, even the hard ones, are as ordinary in the run of things as a rose in spring or fruit in summer. Surprise is optional once you remember the seasons.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Let that of Heraclitus never be out of thy mind, that the death of earth, is water, and the death of water, is air; and the death of air, is fire; and so on the contrary.
plain: Keep in mind the old picture where earth passes into water, water into air, and air into fire, then back again. Endings are changes of form, which eases some of the sting.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Even as if any of the gods should tell thee, Thou shalt certainly die to-morrow, or next day, thou wouldst not, except thou wert extremely base and pusillanimous, take it for a great benefit, rather to die the next day after, than to-morrow; (for alas, what is the difference!) so, for the same reason, think it no great matter to die rather many years after, than the very next day.
plain: If death were tomorrow or the day after, that extra day would be a thin gift. Many added years are, by the same measure, less of a prize than they feel now.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Let it be thy perpetual meditation, how many physicians who once looked so grim, and so theatrically shrunk their brows upon their patients, are dead and gone themselves.
plain: Keep recalling how many stern doctors, frowning theatrically over their patients, are themselves dead and gone. The serious face at work does not hold anyone here a day longer.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: If to understand and to be reasonable be common unto all men, then is that reason, for which we are termed reasonable, common unto all.
plain: Shared thinking is what makes people reasonable, so that capacity is common property among us. A colleague or a neighbour has the same basic capacity you are using now.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Thou must be like a promontory of the sea, against which though the waves beat continually, yet it both itself stands, and about it are those swelling waves stilled and quieted.
plain: Be like a headland that waves strike again and again, yet it stays standing and the swell around it grows quiet. Family rows and pressure at work can meet that same steadiness.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Oh, wretched I, to whom this mischance is happened! nay, happy I, to whom this thing being happened, I can continue without grief; neither wounded by that which is present, nor in fear of that which is to come.
plain: When a mishap lands, drop the wretched story and carry on with no grief. Unhurt by what is here, and unafraid of what may follow, you are steadier than it looks.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: It is but an ordinary coarse one, yet it is a good effectual remedy against the fear of death, for a man to consider in his mind the examples of such, who greedily and covetously (as it were) did for a long time enjoy their lives.
plain: Plain remedies for fearing death include picturing people who clung to life and grabbed at it for years. Long possession did not make the leaving softer, which puts the fear in proportion.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Let thy course ever be the most compendious way. The most compendious, is that which is according to nature: that is, in all both words and deeds, ever to follow that which is most sound and perfect. For such a resolution will free a man from all trouble, strife, dissembling, and ostentation.
plain: The shortest honest route is the one that matches how things actually work. Say what you mean and do the next useful thing, and a lot of fuss, pretence, and showing off drops away.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: As generation is, so also death, a secret of nature's wisdom: a mixture of elements, resolved into the same elements again, a thing surely which no man ought to be ashamed of: in a series of other fatal events and consequences, which a rational creature is subject unto, not improper or incongruous, nor contrary to the natural and proper constitution of man himself.
plain: Dying is part of the same order that brought you here, a mixing and unmixing of ordinary stuff. There is nothing shameful in it, and it sits with everything else a person has to meet.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Such and such things, from such and such causes, must of necessity proceed. He that would not have such things to happen, is as he that would have the fig-tree grow without any sap or moisture. In sum, remember this, that within a very little while, both thou and he shall both be dead, and after a little while more, not so much as your names and memories shall be remaining.
plain: Things follow from what came before them, the way a plant needs water to grow. Before long both you and the person annoying you will be gone, and even the names will fade.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Let opinion be taken away, and no man will think himself wronged. If no man shall think himself wronged, then is there no more any such thing as wrong. That which makes not man himself the worse, cannot make his life the worse, neither can it hurt him either inwardly or outwardly. It was expedient in nature that it should be so, and therefore necessary.
plain: Drop the story that you have been wronged, and the sting of the injury often goes with it. What leaves your character untouched does not ruin the day, however awkward the event feels.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Whatsoever doth happen in the world, doth happen justly, and so if thou dost well take heed, thou shalt find it.
plain: If you look closely at what actually happened, it usually fits the way events run, even when it feels unfair. Take a moment before you decide the world has singled you out.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Conceit no such things, as he that wrongeth thee conceiveth, or would have thee to conceive, but look into the matter itself, and see what it is in very truth.
plain: Skip the story the other person wants you to swallow about this row. Look at what actually took place, at work or at home, and name it plainly before you react.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: In the morning when thou findest thyself unwilling to rise, consider with thyself presently, it is to go about a man's work that I am stirred up.
plain: When the alarm goes and the bed feels warmer than the day, remember you are getting up for ordinary work that belongs to you. That is reason enough to put your feet down.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Thou must comfort thyself in the expectation of thy natural dissolution, and in the meantime not grieve at the delay; but rest contented in those two things.
plain: You can settle with the fact that life ends, and also stop fretting that it has not ended yet. Those two acceptances are enough to rest on while the ordinary days continue.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: What is the use that now at this present I make of my soul? Thus from time to time and upon all occasions thou must put this question to thyself; what is now that part of mine which they call the rational mistress part, employed about? Whose soul do I now properly possess? a child's? or a youth's? a woman's? or a tyrant's? some brute, or some wild beast's soul?
plain: Pause now and then and ask what your mind is actually doing. It might be sulking like a child, chasing praise, bossing people, or staying steady enough to choose well.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: What those things are in themselves, which by the greatest part are esteemed good, thou mayest gather even from this.
plain: You can tell what most people call success by watching what they chase. Status, comfort, and being noticed often look shiny until you ask whether they make anyone kinder at home.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: All that I consist of, is either form or matter. No corruption can reduce either of these unto nothing: for neither did I of nothing become a subsistent creature.
plain: You are shape and stuff, and neither of those disappears into a blank. What changes form still belongs to the world, so there is no need to treat an ending as total erasure.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Reason, and rational power, are faculties which content themselves with themselves, and their own proper operations.
plain: Clear thinking is satisfied by doing its own job well. It does not need applause from the group chat or a reward from the office to count as having worked.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Such as thy thoughts and ordinary cogitations are, such will thy mind be in time.
plain: The thoughts you repeat on the commute and late at night slowly become the shape of your mind. Choose the ones you rehearse, because habit builds the person you meet in the mirror.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: To desire things impossible is the part of a mad man. But it is a thing impossible, that wicked man should not commit some such things.
plain: Wanting other people to stop being difficult is a wish that cannot be granted. People who act badly will keep doing it, so plan your evening around that fact instead of raging at it.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: After one consideration, man is nearest unto us; as we are bound to do them good, and to bear with them.
plain: Other people are the closest thing to you, which is why patience with them matters. Do them a good turn when you can, and put up with the ordinary friction of family life.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Honour that which is chiefest and most powerful in the world, and that is it, which makes use of all things, and governs all things. So also in thyself; honour that which is chiefest, and most powerful; and is of one kind and nature with that which we now spake of. For it is the very same, which being in thee, turneth all other things to its own use, and by whom also thy life is governed.
plain: Respect the part of you that can steer the rest, the same way the larger order uses everything for its work. Let that steady part run your day rather than every passing mood.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: That which doth not hurt the city itself; cannot hurt any citizen. This rule thou must remember to apply and make use of upon every conceit and apprehension of wrong.
plain: If something does not damage the community you belong to, it has not really damaged you as a member of it. Try that test when a slight at work feels personal.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: How easy a thing is it for a man to put off from him all turbulent adventitious imaginations, and presently to be in perfect rest and tranquillity!
plain: It is surprisingly easy to set down the noisy pictures in your head and feel quiet again. You do not have to chase every worry the phone throws up before the evening can settle.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Let not that chief commanding part of thy soul be ever subject to any variation through any corporal either pain or pleasure, neither suffer it to be mixed with these, but let it both circumscribe itself, and confine those affections to their own proper parts and members.
plain: Keep the part that decides separate from bodily aches and from the pull of pleasure. Let the body have its signals, while your judgement stays steady enough for the next sensible choice.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: To live with the Gods. He liveth with the Gods, who at all times affords unto them the spectacle of a soul, both contented and well pleased with whatsoever is afforded, or allotted unto her; and performing whatsoever is pleasing to that Spirit, whom (being part of himself) Jove hath appointed to every man as his overseer and governor.
plain: Living well means being content with what you have been given and doing the work that your better judgement approves. Friends and family can see that steadiness more clearly than any speech about it.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Be not angry neither with him whose breath, neither with him whose arm holes, are offensive.
plain: There is no point getting cross because someone near you smells unpleasant. Bodies do that, on the train and in a crowded kitchen, and anger will not change a fact so ordinary.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: 'Where there shall neither roarer be, nor harlot.' Why so? As thou dost purpose to live, when thou hast retired thyself to some such place, where neither roarer nor harlot is: so mayest thou here.
plain: You tell yourself you will behave once you are somewhere quieter, away from loud nights and messy company. You can practise that same restraint here, in the life you already have.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: That rational essence by which the universe is governed, is for community and society; and therefore hath it both made the things that are worse, for the best, and hath allied and knit together those which are best, as it were in an harmony.
plain: The order of things favours people living together, not apart. Even the rough bits get used, and the better parts of a household or a team fit each other when they are allowed to.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: How hast thou carried thyself hitherto towards the Gods? towards thy parents? towards thy brethren? towards thy wife? towards thy children? towards thy masters? thy foster-fathers? thy friends? thy domestics? thy servants?
plain: Ask how you have treated the people closest to you. Parents, partner, children, friends, and the colleagues you rely on will tell you more about your conduct than any private opinion of yourself.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Why should imprudent unlearned souls trouble that which is both learned, and prudent? And which is that that is so? she that understandeth the beginning and the end, and hath the true knowledge of that rational essence, that passeth through all things subsisting, and through all ages being ever the same, disposing and dispensing as it were this universe by certain periods of time.
plain: A mind that sees the larger pattern need not be thrown by people who do not. Noise from the group or the news can pass while you keep hold of what matters.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Within a very little while, thou wilt be either ashes, or a sceletum; and a name perchance; and perchance, not so much as a name.
plain: Before long there will be little left of you but remains and perhaps a name, and perhaps not even that. Remembering this makes office pride and evening worries look smaller than they feel.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Thou mayest always speed, if thou wilt but make choice of the right way; if in the course both of thine opinions and actions, thou wilt observe a true method.
plain: You can keep moving well if you pick the sound path and stick to it in what you think and what you do. Method matters more than mood when the week gets messy.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: If this neither be my wicked act, nor an act anyways depending from any wickedness of mine, and that by it the public is not hurt; what doth it concern me?
plain: If you did not cause the mess, it did not spring from a fault of yours, and nobody else is harmed, you can let it go. Not every group chat drama is yours to carry.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Think thyself fit and worthy to speak, or to do anything that is according to nature, and let not the reproach, or report of some that may ensue upon it, ever deter thee.
plain: Consider yourself able to say and do the decent thing, and do not let gossip afterwards put you off. A snide comment in the office is a poor reason to abandon a fair action.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Let death surprise me when it will, and where it will, I may be εὔμοιρος, or a happy man, nevertheless. For he is a happy man, who in his lifetime dealeth unto himself a happy lot and portion. A happy lot and portion is, good inclinations of the soul, good desires, good actions.
plain: Whenever the end comes, a person can still have lived well by giving themselves sound aims, decent wants, and decent actions. That private lot is what makes the years count.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: I continue my course by actions according to nature, until I fall and cease, breathing out my last breath into that air, by which continually breathed in I did live; and falling upon that earth, out of whose gifts and fruits my father gathered his seed, my mother her blood, and my nurse her milk, out of which for so many years I have been provided, both of meat and drink.
plain: Keep acting in a fitting way until you stop, giving breath back to the air and your body to the ground that fed you. Years of food and care all came from that same place.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: No man can admire thee for thy sharp acute language, such is thy natural disability that way.
plain: Nobody is going to admire you for clever talk if that is not your gift. Put your effort into being reliable at home and at work, where character shows more clearly than wit.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Such there be, who when they have done a good turn to any, are ready to set them on the score for it, and to require retaliation.
plain: Some people help you and then keep a tally, waiting to be paid back in favours. A kindness that comes with a bill is really a transaction, and you can notice that without playing along.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: The form of the Athenians' prayer did run thus: 'O rain, rain, good Jupiter, upon all the grounds and fields that belong to the Athenians.' Either we should not pray at all, or thus absolutely and freely; and not every one for himself in particular alone.
plain: The old civic wish asked for rain on everybody's fields, not just one farm. If you hope for something, hope it for the whole street or the whole team, rather than only for yourself.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: As we say commonly, The physician hath prescribed unto this man, riding; unto another, cold baths; unto a third, to go barefoot: so it is alike to say, The nature of the universe hath prescribed unto this man sickness, or blindness, or some loss, or damage or some such thing.
plain: A doctor sets one person exercise, another cold water, another walking without shoes. In a similar way, illness, loss, or damage can be what your stretch of life has been given to work with.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: The matter itself, of which the universe doth consist, is of itself very tractable and pliable. That rational essence that doth govern it, hath in itself no cause to do evil. It hath no evil in itself; neither can it do anything that is evil: neither can anything be hurt by it. And all things are done and determined according to its will and prescript.
plain: The stuff of the world is workable, and the order running it has no malice in it. Nothing it brings is meant as harm, so you can meet events without assuming a plot against you.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: If it were that thou hadst at one time both a stepmother, and a natural mother living, thou wouldst honour and respect her also; nevertheless to thine own natural mother would thy refuge, and recourse be continually.
plain: If you had a stepmother and your own mother, you would be civil to one and still go home to the other. Treat status that way, and keep returning to what steadies you.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: How marvellous useful it is for a man to represent unto himself meats, and all such things that are for the mouth, under a right apprehension and imagination! as for example: This is the carcass of a fish; this of a bird; and this of a hog.
plain: It helps to see fancy food as what it is before the menu flatters you. A dressed plate is still fish or meat, and the craving shrinks once you name it plainly.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Those things which the common sort of people do admire, are most of them such things as are very general, and may be comprehended under things merely natural, or naturally affected and qualified: as stones, wood, figs, vines, olives.
plain: Most of what crowds admire is ordinary material dressed up. Stone, wood, fruit, and vines do not become profound because a shop window or a feed puts them on a pedestal.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Some things hasten to be, and others to be no more. And even whatsoever now is, some part thereof hath already perished.
plain: Some things rush into being and others rush to be gone, and whatever is here has already started to pass. Your plans for the week are changing even while you look at them.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Under, above, and about, are the motions of the elements; but the motion of virtue, is none of those motions, but is somewhat more excellent and divine. Whose way (to speed and prosper in it) must be through a way, that is not easily comprehended.
plain: Materials shift up, down, and around, but decent conduct moves on a different track. That track is harder to see, and still it is the one that makes a day feel properly spent.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Who can choose but wonder at them? They will not speak well of them that are at the same time with them, and live with them; yet they themselves are very ambitious, that they that shall follow, whom they have never seen, nor shall ever see, should speak well of them. As if a man should grieve that he hath not been commended by them, that lived before him.
plain: People refuse to speak well of those living beside them, yet they long for praise from strangers not yet born. That is as odd as feeling hurt that the dead never clapped for you.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Do not ever conceive anything impossible to man, which by thee cannot, or not without much difficulty be effected; but whatsoever in general thou canst Conceive possible and proper unto any man, think that very possible unto thee also.
plain: Do not write off a task as beyond you just because it would be hard. If some other person can do it, you can treat it as possible for you as well, and start there.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Suppose that at the palestra somebody hath all to-torn thee with his nails, and hath broken thy head.
plain: If someone clips you in a game and you end up sore, you treat it as part of playing. Everyday rudeness can be met the same way, without turning a scrape into a feud.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Be it all one unto thee, whether half frozen or well warm; whether only slumbering, or after a full sleep; whether discommended or commended thou do thy duty: or whether dying or doing somewhat else; for that also 'to die,' must among the rest be reckoned as one of the duties and actions of our lives.
plain: Do your part whether you are cold or warm, half awake or rested, blamed or praised. Even stopping for good belongs among the ordinary tasks of a life, not outside them.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: If anybody shall reprove me, and shall make it apparent unto me, that in any either opinion or action of mine I do err, I will most gladly retract. For it is the truth that I seek after, by which I am sure that never any man was hurt; and as sure, that he is hurt that continueth in any error, or ignorance whatsoever.
plain: If someone shows you a mistake in what you think or do, be glad to change it. Truth has never injured a person, while staying with a known error quietly does.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: I for my part will do what belongs unto me; as for other things, whether things unsensible or things irrational; or if rational, yet deceived and ignorant of the true way, they shall not trouble or distract me.
plain: Do the part that is yours, and leave the rest alone. Senseless events, muddled people, and those who have lost the plot need not run your evening or your temper.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Alexander of Macedon, and he that dressed his mules, when once dead both came to one.
plain: A famous ruler and the person who looked after his animals ended in the same place once they died. Rank at work will not travel with you past that point, so wear it lightly.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: if any should put this question unto thee, how this word Antoninus is written, wouldst thou not presently fix thine intention upon it, and utter out in order every letter of it?
plain: If someone asked you to spell a familiar name, you would slow down and give each letter in order. Bring that same care to the next task, one step after another, until it is done.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Is it not a cruel thing to forbid men to affect those things, which they conceive to agree best with their own natures, and to tend most to their own proper good and behoof?
plain: It feels harsh to block people from chasing what they believe is good for them. Remember they are following their own picture of benefit, which helps you stay fair when you disagree.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Death is a cessation from the impression of the senses, the tyranny of the passions, the errors of the mind, and the servitude of the body.
plain: Death is the end of sense impressions, of being pushed by strong feelings, of mental mistakes, and of the body's demands. Seen that way, it is a stopping rather than an evening's drama.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: If in this kind of life thy body be able to hold out, it is a shame that thy soul should faint first, and give over, take heed, lest of a philosopher thou become a mere Cæsar in time, and receive a new tincture from the court.
plain: If your body can keep going through a hard stretch, it is a pity if your resolve quits first. Watch that comfort and the habits of a fancy circle do not dye you.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Stir up thy mind, and recall thy wits again from thy natural dreams, and visions, and when thou art perfectly awoken, and canst perceive that they were but dreams that troubled thee, as one newly awakened out of another kind of sleep look upon these worldly things with the same mind as thou didst upon those, that thou sawest in thy sleep.
plain: Rouse yourself from the half-dream you drift in, and notice the worry was only a picture. Look at money and status with the same distance you keep once a bad dream ends.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Look in, let not either the proper quality, or the true worth of anything pass thee, before thou hast fully apprehended it.
plain: Look closely, and do not let the real quality of a thing slide past before you have grasped it. A headline, a compliment, or a bargain deserves a second look before you swallow it.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: As long as the foot doth that which belongeth unto it to do, and the hand that which belongs unto it, their labour, whatsoever it be, is not unnatural.
plain: As long as your foot does a foot's job and your hand does a hand's job, the effort is fitting. The same goes for your role at home or at work.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Asia, Europe; what are they, but as corners of the whole world; of which the whole sea, is but as one drop; and the great Mount Athos, but as a clod, as all present time is but as one point of eternity.
plain: Whole continents are corners, the sea a drop, and a great mountain a lump of earth. This moment is just as small against the long stretch of time, which steadies a frantic week.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Fit and accommodate thyself to that estate and to those occurrences, which by the destinies have been annexed unto thee; and love those men whom thy fate it is to live with; but love them truly.
plain: Settle into the circumstances that have actually been given to you, and care properly for the people you live among. Family and colleagues are not a waiting room for a better cast.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: We all work to one effect, some willingly, and with a rational apprehension of what we do: others without any such knowledge.
plain: Everyone is working for one outcome, some with a clear sense of what they are doing and others without a clue. You can choose to do your share on purpose, at work and at home.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: If so be that the Gods have deliberated in particular of those things that should happen unto me, I must stand to their deliberation, as discrete and wise.
plain: If whatever happens to you was settled with care, you can stand by that settlement instead of fighting it. Meet the day you have been handed, including the dull bits, as something workable.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: All substances come soon to their change, and either they shall be resolved by way of exhalation (if so be that all things shall be reunited into one substance), or as others maintain, they shall be scattered and dispersed.
plain: Everything solid changes before long, either drawn back into one mass or broken up and spread out. Your belongings, your job title, and even your body are already on that path.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Whatsoever in any kind doth happen to any one, is expedient to the whole. And thus much to content us might suffice, that it is expedient for the whole in general.
plain: What happens to any one person serves the larger whole, and that fact can be enough. Your setback at work may be painful and still sit inside a pattern bigger than your week.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: As the ordinary shows of the theatre and of other such places, when thou art presented with them, affect thee; as the same things still seen, and in the same fashion, make the sight ingrateful and tedious; so must all the things that we see all our life long affect us. For all things, above and below, are still the same, and from the same causes. When then will there be an end?
plain: Shows repeat until the novelty wears off and you grow bored of the same scenes. Life is like that too, the same kinds of events from the same causes, so freshness was never the point.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Let the several deaths of men of all sorts, and of all sorts of professions, and of all sort of nations, be a perpetual object of thy thoughts,... so that thou mayst even come down to Philistio, Phœbus, and Origanion.
plain: Keep in mind how people of every job and every background have already died, famous names and forgotten ones alike. That picture makes today's urgency at the office feel less final.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: When thou wilt comfort and cheer thyself, call to mind the several gifts and virtues of them, whom thou dost daily converse with; as for example, the industry of the one; the modesty of another; the liberality of a third; of another some other thing.
plain: When you need a lift, call to mind the good qualities of people you see every day. One person's effort, another's modesty, and another's generosity are already near if you notice.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Dost thou grieve that thou dost weigh but so many pounds, and not three hundred rather? Just as much reason hast thou to grieve that thou must live but so many years, and not longer. For as for bulk and substance thou dost content thyself with that proportion of it that is allotted unto thee, so shouldst thou for time.
plain: You do not mourn weighing less than some huge number, so there is little sense in mourning a limited span of years. Take the time you have the way you take your size.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Let us do our best endeavours to persuade them; but however, if reason and justice lead thee to it, do it, though they be never so much against it.
plain: Try to bring people with you, and if fairness still points a certain way, go that way even when they object. A family decision or a work call does not need unanimous cheers.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: The ambitious supposeth another man's act, praise and applause, to be his own happiness; the voluptuous his own sense and feeling; but he that is wise, his own action.
plain: Someone hungry for status treats other people's applause as their happiness, and someone hungry for pleasure treats a pleasant feeling that way. A wiser measure is your own action, which you can actually steer.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: It is in thy power absolutely to exclude all manner of conceit and opinion, as concerning this matter; and by the same means, to exclude all grief and sorrow from thy soul. For as for the things and objects themselves, they of themselves have no such power, whereby to beget and force upon us any opinion at all.
plain: You can set aside the judgement you have formed about a hard event, and the sorrow tied to that judgement eases. The event itself cannot force a story on you.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Use thyself when any man speaks unto thee, so to hearken unto him, as that in the interim thou give not way to any other thoughts; that so thou mayst (as far as is possible) seem fixed and fastened to his very soul, whosoever he be that speaks unto thee.
plain: When someone speaks to you, listen without drifting into other thoughts, so you are really with them. A friend, a child, or a colleague can tell when your mind has gone back to your phone.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Will either passengers, or patients, find fault and complain, either the one if they be well carried, or the others if well cured? Do they take care for any more than this; the one, that their shipmaster may bring them safe to land, and the other, that their physician may effect their recovery?
plain: Travellers mainly want a safe arrival, and patients mainly want to get well. They are not obliged to cheer the person who simply did the job, so do yours without waiting for extra thanks.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: How many of them who came into the world at the same time when I did, are already gone out of it?
plain: Think how many people born around the same time as you have already left. That plain count, not a speech, is enough to loosen your grip on small slights from today.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: To them that are sick of the jaundice, honey seems bitter; and to them that are bitten by a mad dog, the water terrible; and to children, a little ball seems a fine thing. And why then should I be angry? or do I think that error and false opinion is less powerful to make men transgress, than either choler, being immoderate and excessive, to cause the jaundice; or poison, to cause rage?
plain: To a sick eye honey tastes bitter, and a frightened person can fear plain water, while a child treasures a small ball. False judgement moves people just as strongly, so anger misses the cause.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: No man can hinder thee to live as thy nature doth require. Nothing can happen unto thee, but what the common good of nature doth require.
plain: Nobody can stop you living in the way your nature asks, and nothing can land on you except what the wider order allows. That leaves your conduct, at home or out, still in your hands.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: What manner of men they be whom they seek to please, and what to get, and by what actions: how soon time will cover and bury all things, and how many it hath already buried!
plain: Notice whose approval people chase, what they hope to gain, and what they do to get it. Time covers all of that quickly, and it has already covered more lives than you can picture.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Let this be thy only joy, and thy only comfort, from one sociable kind action without intermission to pass unto another, God being ever in thy mind.
plain: Let your satisfaction come from moving straight from one kind act to the next, without a gap for showing off. Keep that thread going through an ordinary evening with the people around you.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: The rational commanding part, as it alone can stir up and turn itself; so it maketh both itself to be, and everything that happeneth, to appear unto itself, as it will itself.
plain: The part of you that can think can also turn itself, and it decides how events appear. A rough email looks different once you choose the frame rather than the first reaction.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: According to the nature of the universe all things particular are determined, not according to any other nature, either about compassing and containing; or within, dispersed and contained; or without, depending.
plain: Particular things are set by the nature of the whole, not by some separate rule hovering above, inside, or outside it. Your small events belong to that same arrangement, including the inconvenient ones.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Whensoever by some present hard occurrences thou art constrained to be in some sort troubled and vexed, return unto thyself as soon as may be, and be not out of tune longer than thou must needs. For so shalt thou be the better able to keep thy part another time, and to maintain the harmony, if thou dost use thyself to this continually; once out, presently to have recourse unto it, and to begin again.
plain: When a hard moment knocks you off balance, come back to yourself quickly and do not stay jarred. Practise that return, and the next jolt at home or at work finds you quicker.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: What is wickedness? It is that which many time and often thou hast already seen and known in the world.
plain: Wrongdoing is not a new monster. It is the same old pattern you have already met, in the news and in ordinary rooms, so you can recognise it without being stunned.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: As several members in one body united, so are reasonable creatures in a body divided and dispersed, all made and prepared for one common operation.
plain: People are spread out like limbs of one body, separate in place and still made for a shared task. Your work and care fit a larger effort, even when you cannot see it.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Of things that are external, happen what will to that which can suffer by external accidents. Those things that suffer let them complain themselves, if they will; as for me, as long as I conceive no such thing, that that which is happened is evil, I have no hurt; and it is in my power not to conceive any such thing.
plain: Let outside things take the knocks and do the complaining if they must. While you refuse to call the event an evil, it does not injure you, and that refusal stays available.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Whatsoever any man either doth or saith, thou must be good; not for any man's sake, but for thine own nature's sake; as if either gold, or the emerald, or purple, should ever be saying to themselves, Whatsoever any man either doth or saith, I must still be an emerald, and I must keep my colour.
plain: Whatever anyone does or says, stay true to your own nature, the way a gem stays a gem. Talk around you need not change your colour or your conduct.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: This may ever be my comfort and security: my understanding, that ruleth over all, will not of itself bring trouble and vexation upon itself.
plain: The understanding that governs you will not, on its own, drag trouble into itself. If the evening feels stormy, the storm is not being manufactured by the part of you that can still see clearly.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: What is εὐδαιμονία, or happiness: but ἀγαθὸς δαίμων, or, a good dæmon, or spirit?
plain: Happiness is a good spirit in the ordinary sense, a mind in decent shape. It shows up in how you handle a Tuesday, not in a mood you have to chase online.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Is any man so foolish as to fear change, to which all things that once were not owe their being?
plain: Change is the reason anything that once did not exist is here at all, so fearing it is an odd habit. Your job, your body, and your plans are already products of it.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Through the substance of the universe, as through a torrent pass all particular bodies, being all of the same nature, and all joint workers with the universe itself as in one of our bodies so many members among themselves.
plain: Particular lives rush through the stuff of the world like a current, sharing one nature and working as one. You are in that stream with everyone else, not parked beside it.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: The nature of the universe, of the common substance of all things as it were of so much wax hath now perchance formed a horse; and then, destroying that figure, hath new tempered and fashioned the matter of it into the form and substance of a tree: then that again into the form and substance of a man: and then that again into some other.
plain: The same material gets shaped into one thing, then melted and shaped into another, and then another. Nothing you own, and nobody you love, keeps a fixed form for the whole stretch.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: An angry countenance is much against nature, and it is oftentimes the proper countenance of them that are at the point of death.
plain: A furious face goes against a healthy life, and it is often the look of someone near the end. Soften yours at home before a sour evening sets in around you.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Whensoever any man doth trespass against other, presently consider with thyself what it was that he did suppose to be good, what to be evil, when he did trespass.
plain: When someone crosses a line, ask what they thought was good and what they thought was bad at that moment. That question cools a row with a friend faster than a sharp reply.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: What fear is there that thy dogmata, or philosophical resolutions and conclusions, should become dead in thee, and lose their proper power and efficacy to make thee live happy, as long as those proper and correlative fancies, and representations of things on which they mutually depend (which continually to stir up and revive is in thy power,) are still kept fresh and alive?
plain: Your guiding conclusions stay alive while you keep refreshing the pictures they rest on. That refresh is in your hands, on a commute or before sleep, and it keeps them from going stale.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Fancy not to thyself things future, as though they were present but of those that are present, take some aside, that thou takest most benefit of, and consider of them particularly, how wonderfully thou wouldst want them, if they were not present.
plain: Do not treat tomorrow's worries as if they were already here. Take one good thing in the room, a person or a quiet hour, and notice how you would miss it.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Wipe off all opinion stay the force and violence of unreasonable lusts and affections: circumscribe the present time examine whatsoever it be that is happened, either to thyself or to another: divide all present objects, either in that which is formal or material think of the last hour.
plain: Clear away hasty judgements, check unruly wants, and stay with this hour. Look at what has happened piece by piece, and let the thought of a last hour shrink what does not matter.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: All things (saith he) are by certain order and appointment. And what if the elements only.
plain: Things arrive by some order, even if you only grant that to the elements themselves. Either way, the mess on your desk is not a private exception to how the world behaves.

author: Marcus Aurelius
