text: Out of Plato. 'He then whose mind is endowed with true magnanimity, who hath accustomed himself to the contemplation both of all times, and of all things in general; can this mortal life (thinkest thou) seem any great matter unto him?
plain: Someone used to looking across long stretches of time and the range of things will not find one human life a huge affair. Your own busy week sits inside that wide view.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Out of Antisthenes. 'It is a princely thing to do well, and to be ill-spoken of.
plain: It is a strong thing to act well and still be badly spoken about afterwards. Let the criticism come, at work or among friends, and keep the action clean.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Out of several poets and comics. 'It will but little avail thee, to turn thine anger and indignation upon the things themselves that have fallen across unto thee.
plain: Getting angry at the objects and events that have crossed you does very little good. A late train or a blunt text will not improve because you stand there glaring.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Out of Plato. 'My answer, full of justice and equity, should be this: Thy speech is not right, O man! if thou supposest that he that is of any worth at all, should apprehend either life or death, as a matter of great hazard and danger; and should not make this rather his only care, to examine his own actions, whether just or unjust: whether actions of a good, or of a wicked man, &c.
plain: A person of any worth does not treat living or dying as the great danger. The real care is to check whether one's actions are fair or foul, today, in ordinary dealings.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: To look back upon things of former ages, as upon the manifold changes and conversions of several monarchies and commonwealths.
plain: Look back at earlier ages and the rise and fall of governments, and the present fuss shrinks. Empires changed hands, and your current worry at work will pass in the same broad way.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: He hath a stronger body, and is a better wrestler than I. What then? Is he more bountiful? is he more modest? Doth he bear all adverse chances with more equanimity: or with his neighbour's offences with more meekness and gentleness than I?
plain: Someone may be stronger than you and better in a contest. Ask instead whether they are more generous, more modest, or gentler when a neighbour gives offence, which is the comparison that counts.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Where the matter may be effected agreeably to that reason, which both unto the Gods and men is common, there can be no just cause of grief or sorrow.
plain: Where something can be handled in line with the reason people share, there is no solid ground for sorrow about it. Do the fair thing, then leave the ache out of the evening.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: That which most men would think themselves most happy for, and would prefer before all things, if the Gods would grant it unto them after their deaths, thou mayst whilst thou livest grant unto thyself; to live again.
plain: What many people would beg to be given after they die, another chance to live, you can give yourself now. Use the day in front of you as that second life, starting with this evening.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Look not about upon other men's minds and understandings; but look right on forwards whither nature, both that of the universe, in those things that happen unto thee; and thine in particular, in those things that are done by thee: doth lead, and direct thee.
plain: Stop glancing sideways at how other people think, and look ahead along the path in front of you. Follow what events require, and follow what your own nature requires in what you do.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: As one who had lived, and were now to die by right, whatsoever is yet remaining, bestow that wholly as a gracious overplus upon a virtuous life.
plain: Live as someone who has already had a full life and could rightly stop. Treat whatever time is left as an extra gift, and spend it on conduct you can respect.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Thou must use thyself also to keep thy body fixed and steady; free from all loose fluctuant either motion, or posture. And as upon thy face and looks, thy mind hath easily power over them to keep them to that which is grave and decent; so let it challenge the same power over the whole body also. But so observe all things in this kind, as that it be without any manner of affectation.
plain: Train your body to stay steady, without fidgety movement or a sloppy stance. Your mind already settles your face, so let it settle the rest of you too, quietly, with no performance for the room.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: The art of true living in this world is more like a wrestler's, than a dancer's practice. For in this they both agree, to teach a man whatsoever falls upon him, that he may be ready for it, and that nothing may cast him down.
plain: Living well is closer to a wrestler's training than a dancer's routine, because you cannot script every move. You learn to meet whatever lands on you, at work or at home, without being flattened.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Thou must continually ponder and consider with thyself, what manner of men they be, and for their minds and understandings what is their present estate, whose good word and testimony thou dost desire.
plain: Keep asking what sort of people they are, and what state their minds are in, when you want their good opinion. Chasing praise from a muddled crowd is a poor use of an evening.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: What pain soever thou art in, let this presently come to thy mind, that it is not a thing whereof thou needest to be ashamed, neither is it a thing whereby thy understanding, that hath the government of all, can be made worse.
plain: Whatever pain you are in, it is not something to be ashamed of, and it cannot spoil the understanding that governs you. The ache is real, and your judgement can still stay intact.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Take heed lest at any time thou stand so affected, though towards unnatural evil men, as ordinary men are commonly one towards another.
plain: Be careful not to sink to the level of petty mutual scorn, even with people who behave badly. Ordinary tit for tat is catching, in a group chat as much as in a kitchen.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: How know we whether Socrates were so eminent indeed, and of so extraordinary a disposition?
plain: We cannot be sure a famous wise person was quite as remarkable as the stories say. That uncertainty is useful, because it sends you back to your own conduct instead of hero worship.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: For it is a thing very possible, that a man should be a very divine man, and yet be altogether unknown.
plain: It is entirely possible to be a deeply good person and still be unknown. No feed needs to notice you, and a quiet life among family can be a complete one.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Free from all compulsion in all cheerfulness and alacrity thou mayst run out thy time, though men should exclaim against thee never so much, and the wild beasts should pull in sunder the poor members of thy pampered mass of flesh.
plain: You can finish your time lightly and in good humour, without being forced, even if people shout and your body takes a battering. Their noise does not have to set your mood.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Word after word, every one by itself, must the things that are spoken be conceived and understood; and so the things that are done, purpose after purpose, every one by itself likewise.
plain: Take what people say one phrase at a time, and take what they do one aim at a time. Slowing down like that stops you inventing a whole drama from a single text.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Then hath a man attained to the estate of perfection in his life and conversation, when he so spends every day, as if it were his last day: never hot and vehement in his affections, nor yet so cold and stupid as one that had no sense; and free from all manner of dissimulation.
plain: You are in good shape when you spend each day as though it might be the last, neither worked up nor numb. Drop the pretence with family and friends.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Can the Gods, who are immortal, for the continuance of so many ages bear without indignation with such and so many sinners, as have ever been, yea not only so, but also take such care for them, that they want nothing; and dust thou so grievously take on, as one that could bear with them no longer; thou that art but for a moment of time? yea thou that art one of those sinners thyself?
plain: If the long order of things can bear countless faults and still provide, you can bear people for a short while. You share their faults, and patience can last an evening.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: What object soever, our reasonable and sociable faculty doth meet with, that affords nothing either for the satisfaction of reason, or for the practice of charity, she worthily doth think unworthy of herself.
plain: When a situation offers nothing for clear thought and nothing for kindness, a sound mind treats it as beneath notice. You can scroll past it, or leave the row, without losing anything that matters.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: When thou hast done well, and another is benefited by thy action, must thou like a very fool look for a third thing besides, as that it may appear unto others also that thou hast done well, or that thou mayest in time, receive one good turn for another?
plain: Once you have acted well and someone has gained by it, stop hunting for a bonus. You do not need an audience, or a favour returned, for the action to have been enough.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: The nature of the universe did once certainly before it was created, whatsoever it hath done since, deliberate and so resolve upon the creation of the world.
plain: The order of things settled, before any of this stood here, that a world would exist. Your small life sits inside that decision, so get on with an ordinary Tuesday.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Let not things future trouble thee. For if necessity so require that they come to pass, thou shalt (whensoever that is) be provided for them with the same reason, by which whatsoever is now present, is made both tolerable and acceptable unto thee.
plain: Leave future events alone. If they have to arrive, you will meet them with the same good sense that makes today bearable, whether that is a work problem or a family one.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Whatsoever is material, doth soon vanish away into the common substance of the whole; and whatsoever is formal, or, whatsoever doth animate that which is material, is soon resumed into the common reason of the whole; and the fame and memory of anything, is soon swallowed up by the general age and duration of the whole.
plain: Stuff fades back into the shared material of things, and the pattern of a life folds back into the shared order. Reputation is swallowed the same way, faster than a feed would have you think.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: To a reasonable creature, the same action is both according to nature, and according to reason.
plain: For a thinking person, an action that fits reason also fits nature, and the two are the same move. Choosing fairly at home is not an extra ideal pasted on top of ordinary life.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: This also, among other things, may serve to keep thee from vainglory; if thou shalt consider, that thou art now altogether incapable of the commendation of one, who all his life long, or from his youth at least, hath lived a philosopher's life.
plain: One check on vanity is to admit you have not lived with steady wisdom from youth, so you cannot expect the praise owed to someone who has. Get on with today's conduct without the costume.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: This, what is it in itself, and by itself, according to its proper constitution? What is the substance of it? What is the matter, or proper use? What is the form or efficient cause? What is it for in this world, and how long will it abide? Thus must thou examine all things, that present themselves unto thee.
plain: Ask of each thing what it is on its own, what it is made of, what it is for, and how long it lasts. A purchase or a craving looks plainer after that.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: When thou art hard to be stirred up and awaked out of thy sleep, admonish thyself and call to mind, that, to perform actions tending to the common good is that which thine own proper constitution, and that which the nature of man do require. But to sleep, is common to unreasonable creatures also. And what more proper and natural, yea what more kind and pleasing, than that which is according to nature?
plain: When you struggle to wake, remember that useful action for others is what a human life asks. Sleep is shared with animals, while getting up to help is the part that fits you.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: As every fancy and imagination presents itself unto thee, consider (if it be possible) the true nature, and the proper qualities of it, and reason with thyself about it.
plain: Whenever a picture pops into your head, pause and ask what it really is and what qualities it has. Do that with a worry, a craving, or a slight, before it runs the next hour.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: At thy first encounter with any one, say presently to thyself: This man, what are his opinions concerning that which is good or evil? as concerning pain, pleasure, and the causes of both; concerning honour, and dishonour, concerning life and death? thus and thus.
plain: At a first meeting, quietly ask what this person counts as good or bad, including pain, pleasure, honour, and death. Their answers, spoken or not, tell you how the evening may go.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Remember, that to change thy mind upon occasion, and to follow him that is able to rectify thee, is equally ingenuous, as to find out at the first, what is right and just, without help. For of thee nothing is required, ti, is beyond the extent of thine own deliberation and jun. merit, and of thine own understanding.
plain: Changing your mind when someone can set you straight is as honest as getting it right alone. Nothing more is asked than that you use your own judgement and think the matter through.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: If it were thine act and in thine own power, wouldest thou do it? If it were not, whom dost tin accuse? the atoms, or the Gods? For to do either, the part of a mad man. Thou must therefore blame nobody, but if it be in thy power, redress what is amiss; if it be not, to what end is it to complain? For nothing should be done but to some certain end.
plain: If the fault is yours and you can act, put it right, and if it is not, blame goes nowhere. Fix what you can and drop complaints you cannot use, because fuss needs a purpose.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Whatsoever dieth and falleth, however and wheresoever it die and fall, it cannot fall out of the world, here it have its abode and change, here also shall it have its dissolution into its proper elements. The same are the world's elements, and the elements of which thou dost consist. And they when they are changed, they murmur not; why shouldest thou?
plain: Whatever ends still stays inside the world and breaks back into the same basic stuff you are made of. Those pieces do not complain when they change, and you need not complain either.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Whatsoever is, was made for something: as a horse, a vine. Why wonderest thou? The sun itself will say of itself, I was made for something; and so hath every god its proper function. What then were then made for? to disport and delight thyself? See how even common sense and reason cannot brook it.
plain: Everything has a job, a horse, a vine, even the daylight. You were not made merely to amuse yourself, and ordinary sense balks at a life spent only on that.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Nature hath its end as well in the end and final consummation of anything that is, as in the begin-nine and continuation of it.
plain: The natural course includes the finish of a thing as much as its start and its middle. An ending, in work or in a life, is part of the shape.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: As one that tosseth up a ball. And what is a ball the better, if the motion of it be upwards; or the worse if it be downwards; or if it chance to fall upon the ground?
plain: A ball is no better for travelling upwards and no worse for coming down or hitting the ground. Treat ups and downs in your week the same way, without ranking yourself by the bounce.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Upon every action that thou art about, put this question to thyself; How will this when it is done agree with me?
plain: Before each action, ask how it will sit with you once it is done. That check helps at the end of work, and in the evening when a habit offers an easy yes.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: That which must be the subject of thy consideration, is either the matter itself, or the dogma, or the operation, or the true sense and signification.
plain: What you need to examine is the thing itself, the judgement you hold about it, the action, or the real meaning. Pick one of those four and you will see the situation more clearly.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Most justly have these things happened unto thee: why dost not thou amend? O but thou hadst rather become good to-morrow, than to be so to-day.
plain: What has happened fits the situation you are in, so ask why you do not correct yourself today. Waiting until tomorrow to improve is only a delay in disguise.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Shall I do it? I will; so the end of my action be to do good unto men. Doth anything by way of cross or adversity happen unto me? I accept it, with reference unto the Gods, and their providence; the fountain of all things, from which whatsoever comes to pass, doth hang and depend.
plain: If an action aims at helping people, go ahead and do it. If something hard arrives, take it as part of the larger order, and carry on with whoever is in front of you.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: By one action judge of the rest: this bathing which usually takes up so much of our time, what is it? Oil, sweat, filth; or the sordes of the body: an excrementitious viscosity, the excrements of oil and other ointments used about the body, and mixed with the sordes of the body: all base and loathsome. And such almost is every part of our life; and every worldly object.
plain: Judge the rest of life by a session that looks luxurious and is mostly oil, sweat, and grime. A lot of glossy pleasures, once you look straight at them, are just as plain and messy.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Lucilla buried Verus; then was Lucilla herself buried by others. So Secunda Maximus, then Secunda herself.
plain: One person buries a partner, and then someone else buries them, and the same pattern repeats through families. Remembering that chain makes status and hurry look thinner than they do on a busy day.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: The true joy of a man, is to do that which properly belongs unto a man. That which is most proper unto a man, is, first, to be kindly affected towards them that are of the same kind and nature as he is himself to contemn all sensual motions and appetites, to discern rightly all plausible fancies and imaginations, to contemplate the nature of the universe; both it, and things that are done in it.
plain: Real satisfaction is doing what fits a person. Be kind to others, see through tempting pictures, set appetite in its place, and keep an eye on the larger world you belong to.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: If pain be an evil, either it is in regard of the body; (and that cannot be, because the body of itself is altogether insensible:) or in regard of the soul But it is in the power of the soul, to preserve her own peace and tranquillity, and not to suppose that pain is evil.
plain: If pain were a true harm, it would sit in the body, which does not judge, or in the mind, which can keep its peace. You can refuse to class the ache as an evil.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Wipe off all idle fancies, and say unto thyself incessantly; Now if I will, it is in my power to keep out of this my soul all wickedness, all lust, and concupiscences, all trouble and confusion. But on the contrary to behold and consider all things according to their true nature, and to carry myself towards everything according to its true worth. Remember then this thy power that nature hath given thee.
plain: Clear the idle pictures and remember you can keep cruelty, craving, and confusion out of your mind. See things as they are, treat them at their real worth, and use that power through the evening.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Whether thou speak in the Senate or whether thou speak to any particular, let thy speech In always grave and modest. But thou must not openly and vulgarly observe that sound and exact form of speaking, concerning that which is truly good and truly civil; the vanity of the world, and of worldly men: which otherwise truth and reason doth prescribe.
plain: Whether you are speaking to a room or to one person, keep your words serious and modest. Skip the public lecture about how vain everyone else is, which truth does not require you to perform.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Augustus his court; his wife, his daughter, his nephews, his sons-in-law his sister, Agrippa, his kinsmen, his domestics, his friends; Areus, Mæcenas, his slayers of beasts for sacrifice and divination: there thou hast the death of a whole court together.
plain: A whole famous household, partners, children, friends, and staff, is gone. Picturing that complete disappearance makes today's scramble for notice look brief, which is a useful scale for a restless evening.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Alexander, Caius, Pompeius; what are these to Diogenes, Heraclitus, and Socrates? These penetrated into the true nature of things; into all causes, and all subjects: and upon these did they exercise their power and authority. But as for those, as the extent of their error was, so far did their slavery extend.
plain: Conquerors look large until you set them beside people who actually understood things. The reach of those rulers' confusion was the reach of their bondage, while clear sight was the freer life.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Contract thy whole life to the measure and proportion of one single action. And if in every particular action thou dost perform what is fitting to the utmost of thy power, let it suffice thee.
plain: Shrink the whole of life down to the size of one action. If in that action you do what fits, as well as you can, let that be enough for the hour you are in.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Receive temporal blessings without ostentation, when they are sent and thou shalt be able to part with them with all readiness and facility when they are taken from thee again.
plain: Take good things that arrive, money, praise, or luck, without showing off, and you will be able to let them go when they leave. Hold them lightly enough for an ordinary week.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Let not the general representation unto thyself of the wretchedness of this our mortal life, trouble thee.
plain: Do not let a sweeping picture of how hard life is weigh you down. Deal with the hour in front of you, a task or a conversation, and leave the grand gloom aside.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: What? are either Panthea or Pergamus abiding to this day by their masters' tombs? or either Chabrias or Diotimus by that of Adrianus?
plain: The devoted attendants are not still waiting beside the graves of the powerful. Loyalty and fame both move on, which is worth recalling when you fret about being remembered at work.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: If thou beest quick-sighted, be so in matter of judgment, and best discretion, saith he.
plain: If you are sharp-eyed, use that sharpness in judgement and in good sense. Spotting flaws around you is easy, so turn the same eye onto your own next choice.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: In the whole constitution of man, I see not any virtue contrary to justice, whereby it may be resisted and opposed. But one whereby pleasure and voluptuousness may be resisted and opposed, I see: continence.
plain: Nothing in a person's makeup cancels fairness, but self-command can stand up to pleasure. Use it when a pleasant pull argues with what is right, especially on a loose evening.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: If thou canst but withdraw conceit and opinion concerning that which may seem hurtful and offensive, thou thyself art as safe, as safe may be. Thou thyself? and who is that? Thy reason. 'Yea, but I am not reason.' Well, be it so. However, let not thy reason or understanding admit of grief, and if there be anything in thee that is grieved, let that, (whatsoever it be,) conceive its own grief, if it can.
plain: Withdraw the judgement that something is harmful, and you stay as safe as can be, since reason need not take on the grief. If another part aches, let it carry that without dragging you down.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: That which is a hindrance of the senses, is an evil to the sensitive nature. That which is a hindrance of the appetitive and prosecutive faculty, is an evil to the sensitive nature.
plain: What blocks the senses troubles the sensing side of you, and what blocks appetite troubles the wanting side. Name which part is hindered before you call the whole day ruined.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: What they have done, they will still do, although thou shouldst hang thyself. First; let it not trouble thee.
plain: People will carry on doing what they have been doing, no matter how upset you get about it. Let that fact stop troubling you first, and then decide what you will do with your evening.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Why should I grieve myself; who never did willingly grieve any other! One thing rejoices one and another thing another.
plain: There is little reason to sink into grief when you have not willingly hurt anyone, and people are cheered by different things. Let others have their pleasures while you keep to what actually suits you.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: This time that is now present, bestow thou upon thyself. They that rather hunt for fame after death, do not consider, that those men that shall be hereafter, will be even such, as these whom now they can so hardly bear with.
plain: Give this present time to yourself. People chasing a name after they are gone forget that future crowds will be as hard to live with as the ones they already find difficult.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Take me and throw me where thou wilt: I am indifferent. For there also I shall have that spirit which is within me propitious; that is well pleased and fully contented both in that constant disposition, and with those particular actions, which to its own proper constitution are suitable and agreeable.
plain: You can be set down anywhere and remain unbothered, because your mind can stay content with a steady outlook and with actions that fit it. Place and noise need not wreck that calm.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Is this then a thing of that worth, that for it my soul should suffer, and become worse than it was? as either basely dejected, or disordinately affected, or confounded within itself, or terrified? What can there be, that thou shouldest so much esteem?
plain: Ask whether this thing is worth your mind becoming worse, flattened, disordered, or frightened. Very little that happens in a day, a slight, a loss, a craving, deserves that kind of damage.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Nothing can happen unto thee, which is not incidental unto thee, as thou art a man.
plain: Nothing can land on you that does not belong to human life. Illness, loss, rudeness, and ageing are part of the package, so meet them as things a person can expect.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Remember that thy mind is of that nature as that it becometh altogether unconquerable, when once recollected in herself, she seeks no other content than this, that she cannot be forced: yea though it so fall out, that it be even against reason itself, that it cloth bandy.
plain: Your mind becomes very hard to overthrow once it gathers itself and wants nothing except the fact that it cannot be forced. Even a strong urge can be met from that settled place.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Keep thyself to the first bare and naked apprehensions of things, as they present themselves unto thee, and add not unto them.
plain: Stay with the first plain impression of what is in front of you, and do not pile extra stories on top. The message is just a message until you add a catastrophe in your head.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Is the cucumber bitter? set it away. Brambles are in the way? avoid them. Let this suffice.
plain: If something is unpleasant, set it aside, and if an obstacle is in the path, step round it. That is enough, without a speech, a sulk, or a ruined evening over a small annoyance.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Not to be slack and negligent; or loose, and wanton in thy actions; nor contentious, and troublesome in thy conversation; nor to rove and wander in thy fancies and imaginations. Not basely to contract thy soul; nor boisterously to sally out with it, or furiously to launch out as it were, nor ever to want employment.
plain: Keep your days steady: do the work in front of you, skip pointless rows, and do not let your thoughts drift all evening with nothing useful to show for them.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: That which the nature of the universe doth busy herself about, is; that which is here, to transfer it thither, to change it, and thence again to take it away, and to carry it to another place. So that thou needest not fear any new thing. For all things are usual and ordinary; and all things are disposed by equality.
plain: Change keeps moving things from one place to another, at work and at home, so a new week rarely brings a danger you have never met in some ordinary form.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: 'They kill me, they cut my flesh; they persecute my person with curses.' What then?
plain: People can criticise you, block your plans, or spoil a whole evening, and the useful question is still what you choose to do with the next free hour.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: He that knoweth not what the world is, knoweth not where he himself is. And he that knoweth not what the world was made for, cannot possibly know either what are the qualities, or what is the nature of the world.
plain: If you never pause to ask what your life is for, the job, the family, and the evenings blur, and you cannot tell what actually matters in them.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Not only now henceforth to have a common breath, or to hold correspondency of breath, with that air, that compasseth us about; but to have a common mind, or to hold correspondency of mind also with that rational substance, which compasseth all things.
plain: Breathing the same air as everyone else is the easy part. Sharing a clear and fair mind with people at home and at work takes steady daily practice.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Wickedness in general doth not hurt the world. Particular wickedness doth not hurt any other: only unto him it is hurtful, whosoever he be that offends, unto whom in great favour and mercy it is granted, that whensoever he himself shall but first desire it, he may be presently delivered of it.
plain: A bad habit mostly damages the person keeping it, and the relief is that you can set it down the moment you truly decide the evening will go differently.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: The sun seemeth to be shed abroad. And indeed it is diffused but not effused. For that diffusion of it is a τάσις or an extension.
plain: A good day can look scattered, with messages, tasks, and family all pulling at once, yet it holds together when your effort stays stretched rather than spilled in every direction.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: He that feareth death, either feareth that he shall have no sense at all, or that his senses will not be the same. Whereas, he should rather comfort himself, that either no sense at all, and so no sense of evil; or if any sense, then another life, and so no death properly.
plain: Fear of the end often comes down to dreading a blank or dreading something unfamiliar, and either way the horror you picture at night is larger than the plain fact.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: All men are made one for another: either then teach them better, or bear with them.
plain: People at work and at home will get things wrong. You can show them a kinder way, or you can stay patient while they catch up in their own time.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: The motion of the mind is not as the motion of a dart. For the mind when it is wary and cautelous, and by way of diligent circumspection turneth herself many ways, may then as well be said to go straight on to the object, as when it useth no such circumspection.
plain: Thinking a decision through, checking your diary and asking a friend first, is still moving forward. Careful thought at home or at work is a straight path, not wasted time.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: To pierce and penetrate into the estate of every one's understanding that thou hast to do with: as also to make the estate of thine own open, and penetrable to any other.
plain: Try to see what a colleague or partner actually understands, and let them see your own thinking plainly, so nobody spends the evening guessing across the kitchen table.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Every particular nature hath content, when in its own proper course it speeds. A reasonable nature doth then speed, when first in matter of fancies and imaginations, it gives no consent to that which is either false uncertain.
plain: You feel steadier when you stop agreeing with every worrying story your mind invents, especially late at night when a message or a quiet house makes small fears look huge.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Thou hast no time nor opportunity to read. What then? Hast thou not time and opportunity to exercise thyself, not to wrong thyself; to strive against all carnal pleasures and pains, and to get the upper hand of them; to contemn honour and vainglory; and not only, not to be angry with them, whom towards thee thou doest find unsensible and unthankful; but also to have a care of them still, and of their welfare?
plain: A busy week still leaves room to skip the extra drink, ignore the urge to show off, and stay kind to people who never bother to say thank you.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Forbear henceforth to complain of the trouble of a courtly life, either in public before others, or in private by thyself.
plain: Stop rehearsing how hard the working day is, whether you say it aloud to friends or only turn it over in your head on the train home at night.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Repentance is an inward and self-reprehension for the neglect or omission of somewhat that was profitable. Now whatsoever is good, is also profitable, and it is the part of an honest virtuous man to set by it, and to make reckoning of it accordingly. But never did any honest virtuous man repent of the neglect or omission of any carnal pleasure: no carnal pleasure then is either good or profitable.
plain: People regret skipped duties, missed calls, and broken promises to family. Almost nobody looks back and wishes they had chased one more round of pleasure on a tired evening.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: He that is unjust, is also impious. For the nature of the universe, having made all reasonable creatures one for another, to the end that they should do one another good; more or less according to the several persons and occasions but in nowise hurt one another: it is manifest that he that doth transgress against this her will, is guilty of impiety towards the most ancient and venerable of all the deities.
plain: We are built to help one another, at home and in the street. Treating people badly breaks that basic bond, even on an ordinary evening when nobody official is watching.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Labour not as one to whom it is appointed to be wretched, nor as one that either would be pitied, or admired; but let this be thine only care and desire; so always and in all things to prosecute or to forbear, as the law of charity, or mutual society doth require.
plain: Do the job because it helps the people involved, not so colleagues will pity you or clap. Quiet usefulness at work beats performing how hard you are trying.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: This day I did come out of all my trouble. Nay I have cast out all my trouble; it should rather be for that which troubled thee, whatsoever it was, was not without anywhere that thou shouldest come out of it, but within in thine own opinions, from whence it must be cast out, before thou canst truly and constantly be at ease.
plain: The strain you feel after a long day sits in the story you tell yourself. Ease comes when you drop that story, not when the diary suddenly clears.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: All those things, for matter of experience are usual and ordinary; for their continuance but for a day; and for their matter, most base and filthy. As they were in the days of those whom we have buried, so are they now also, and no otherwise.
plain: The drama that fills a group chat today is the same small stuff people fussed over years ago, and it will feel just as small by tomorrow morning.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: The things themselves that affect us, they stand without doors, neither knowing anything themselves nor able to utter anything unto others concerning themselves. What then is it, that passeth verdict on them? The understanding.
plain: A late email or a sharp comment from a colleague just sits there. Your mind is what decides it is a crisis, or merely something to handle after dinner.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: As virtue and wickedness consist not in passion, but in action; so neither doth the true good or evil of a reasonable charitable man consist in passion, but in operation and action.
plain: What counts is what you do next, the message you send or the help you offer a friend, not the rush of feeling that hits you in the moment.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: To the stone that is cast up, when it comes down it is no hurt unto it; as neither benefit, when it doth ascend.
plain: Up and down days are like a ball tossed in the air. Rising does not make you special, and landing does not mean the whole week is ruined.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Sift their minds and understandings, and behold what men they be, whom thou dost stand in fear of what they shall judge of thee, what they themselves judge of themselves.
plain: Before you dread what friends or colleagues think of you, look at how muddled their own evenings are. Their verdict is rarely as solid as it feels on the day.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: All things that are in the world, are always in the estate of alteration. Thou also art in a perpetual change, yea and under corruption too, in some part: and so is the whole world.
plain: Your body, your job, and the people around you are all shifting a little every month. Nothing in ordinary life stays fixed, including the mood you woke up with.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: it is not thine, but another man's sin. Why should it trouble thee? Let him look to it, whose sin it is.
plain: When a friend messes up, that mistake belongs to them. You can care and still leave the fixing where it actually sits, instead of carrying it all evening.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Of an operation and of a purpose there is an ending, or of an action and of a purpose we say commonly, that it is at an end: from opinion also there is an absolute cessation, which is as it were the death of it.
plain: A plan finishes, a work project ends, and a long grudge can end too. An opinion you keep feeding will fade once you stop giving it your evenings.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: It were indeed more happy and comfortable, for a man to depart out of this world, having lived all his life long clear from all falsehood, dissimulation, voluptuousness, and pride.
plain: A life feels cleaner when you leave out the showing off, the little lies told to family, and the expensive habits that only impress people for a single evening.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: As occasion shall require, either to thine own understanding, or to that of the universe, or to his, whom thou hast now to do with, let thy refuge be with all speed.
plain: When a moment at home or at work gets heated, go straight to your own judgement, to what the situation plainly needs, or to the person standing in front of you.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: As thou thyself, whoever thou art, were made for the perfection and consummation, being a member of it, of a common society; so must every action of thine tend to the perfection and consummation of a life that is truly sociable.
plain: You belong in a shared life with family, friends, and neighbours. Let the next thing you do today make that shared life a bit more workable for everyone.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Children's anger, mere babels; wretched souls bearing up dead bodies, that they may not have their fall so soon: even as it is in that common dirge song.
plain: A flare of anger often has the weight of a child's tantrum, and a lot of adult effort goes into holding up worries that were already finished yesterday.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Go to the quality of the cause from which the effect doth proceed. Behold it by itself bare and naked, separated from all that is material. Then consider the utmost bounds of time that that cause, thus and thus qualified, can subsist and abide.
plain: Strip a worry down to what actually caused it, without the extra drama, and then ask how long that cause can really last across a normal working week.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Infinite are the troubles and miseries, that thou hast already been put to, by reason of this only, because that for all happiness it did not suffice thee, or, that thou didst not account it sufficient happiness, that thy understanding did operate according to its natural constitution.
plain: Most of the strain in a week comes from wanting every day to feel special. It is already enough when your judgement stays straight through an ordinary afternoon at home.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: When any shall either impeach thee with false accusations, or hatefully reproach thee, or shall use any such carriage towards thee, get thee presently to their minds and understandings, and look in them, and behold what manner of men they be.
plain: If someone has a go at you unfairly, look at the kind of day they are having and the habits they live with, before you take their words to heart.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Up and down, from one age to another, go the ordinary things of the world; being still the same.
plain: Fashions, family arguments, and office politics all change their costume, but the same ordinary human mess turns up in every generation, including this one scrolling past on your phone.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Within a while the earth shall cover us all, and then she herself shall have her change.
plain: Soon enough the people fretting tonight in this house and in this office will be gone, and even the streets they worried about will have changed their shape.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: And these your professed politicians, the only true practical philosophers of the world, (as they think of themselves) so full of affected gravity, or such professed lovers of virtue and honesty, what wretches be they in very deed; how vile and contemptible in themselves?
plain: People who perform virtue for a watching audience, at work or online, often look smaller up close, once the serious voice drops and the ordinary evening habits show.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: From some high place as it were to look down, and to behold here flocks, and there sacrifices, without number; and all kind of navigation; some in a rough and stormy sea, and some in a calm: the general differences, or different estates of things, some, that are now first upon being; the several and mutual relations of those things that are together; and some other things that are at their last.
plain: From a little bit of distance, the rush of traffic, family plans, and late-night worries looks like weather passing, some of it just starting and some already fading.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Thou must not in matter of death carry thyself scornfully, but as one that is well pleased with it, as being one of those things that nature hath appointed.
plain: Meeting the end of a life, or the end of a chapter, goes better when you treat it as part of the order of things, not as an insult.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Many of those things that trouble and straiten thee, it is in thy power to cut off, as wholly depending from mere conceit and opinion; and then thou shalt have room enough.
plain: A lot of what tightens your chest is a story you can drop. Once that opinion goes, the evening has more room than it did an hour ago.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: To comprehend the whole world together in thy mind, and the whole course of this present age to represent it unto thyself, and to fix thy thoughts upon the sudden change of every particular object.
plain: Picture the whole of the week, not only this tense hour, and notice how quickly a mood, a plan, or a news alert changes into something else entirely.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: What are their minds and understandings; and what the things that they apply themselves unto: what do they love, and what do they hate for? Fancy to thyself the estate of their souls openly to be seen. When they think they hurt them shrewdly, whom they speak ill of; and when they think they do them a very good turn, whom they commend and extol: O how full are they then of conceit, and opinion!
plain: Watch what people chase and what they sneer at in a group chat. The praise and the gossip they hand out say more about their own vanity than about you.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Loss and corruption, is in very deed nothing else but change and alteration; and that is it, which the nature of the universe doth most delight in, by which, and according to which, whatsoever is done, is well done.
plain: Losing a routine, a role, or a familiar plan is mostly things changing shape. That shift is how ordinary life keeps moving, even when it stings this week.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: How base and putrid, every common matter is! Water, dust, and from the mixture of these bones, and all that loathsome stuff that our bodies do consist of: so subject to be infected, and corrupted.
plain: Human bodies are ordinary materials that tire, ache, and slowly wear out with the years. Remembering that keeps looks, status, and one bad night in a more honest proportion.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Will this querulousness, this murmuring, this complaining and dissembling never be at an end?
plain: There is a point in the day when the sighing, the muttered complaints, and the polished excuses can stop, and the rest of the evening can simply be lived.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: It is all one to see these things for a hundred of years together or but for three years.
plain: Watching the same office dramas and family patterns for three years teaches you as much as watching them for a lifetime. Length does not add a new lesson.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Sayest thou unto that rational part, Thou art dead; corruption hath taken hold on thee? Doth it then also void excrements? Doth it like either oxen, or sheep, graze or feed; that it also should be mortal, as well as the body?
plain: Your judgement is not a body that wears out like knees or appetite. The part of you that chooses can stay clear even when you feel tired and physical.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: He that sinneth, sinneth unto himself. He that is unjust, hurts himself, in that he makes himself worse than he was before. Not he only that committeth, but he also that omitteth something, is oftentimes unjust.
plain: Cutting corners or staying silent when you should speak both land on you. Each one leaves you a little less reliable with the people who depend on you.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Either the Gods can do nothing for us at all, or they can still and allay all the distractions and distempers of thy mind.
plain: Either outside help will not settle your head, or real calm is available and worth using. Either way, the next useful step is quieting the noise yourself tonight.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: It is common to all trades and professions to mind and intend that only, which now they are about, and the instrument whereby they work.
plain: A cook watches the pan, a driver watches the road, and you can do the same with the task in front of you, using attention as the tool.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: When at any time thou art offended with any one's impudency, put presently this question to thyself: 'What?
plain: When sheer cheek from a stranger winds you up in public, ask whether rude people were ever going to disappear from offices, buses, and family chats. They were not.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: If my present apprehension of the object be right, and my present action charitable, and this, towards whatsoever doth proceed from God, be my present disposition, to be well pleased with it, it sufficeth.
plain: If you see the situation clearly, act kindly towards people, and accept what the day has already handed you, that is a complete enough result for one afternoon.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: To wipe away fancy, to use deliberation, to quench concupiscence, to keep the mind free to herself.
plain: Clear the dramatic story, think it through, and cool the craving, whether that is for a drink, a reply, or a bit of praise, so your mind stays yours.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Of all unreasonable creatures, there is but one unreasonable soul; and of all that are reasonable, but one reasonable soul, divided betwixt them all.
plain: People share the same kind of mind, however different the jobs and households look. That is a fair reason to expect sense from yourself on an ordinary Tuesday evening.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Man, God, the world, every one in their kind, bear some fruits. All things have their proper time to bear.
plain: People, families, and even a slow working week all produce something in their own season. Forcing a result before it is ready rarely helps anyone in the household.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Either teach them better if it be in thy power; or if it be not, remember that for this use, to bear with them patiently, was mildness and goodness granted unto thee.
plain: If you can help someone do better, do that. If you cannot, patience with family and colleagues is the skill the situation is quietly asking you to use.

author: Seneca
text: All men, brother Gallio, wish to live happily, but are dull at perceiving exactly what it is that makes life happy: and so far is it from being easy to attain the happiness that the more eagerly a man struggles to reach it the further he departs from it, if he takes the wrong road; for, since this leads in the opposite direction, his very swiftness carries him all the further away.
plain: Almost everyone wants a good life, yet rushing harder down the wrong route, a louder social life or a bigger spend, only carries you further from it each month.

author: Seneca
text: All these are dissipated by virtue, which plucks a man by the ear, and measures the value of pleasures before she permits them to be used; nor does she set much store by those which she allows to pass current, for she merely allows their use, and her cheerfulness is not due to her use of them, but to her moderation in using them.
plain: A steady character checks a pleasure before taking it, including a drink after work, and the good mood comes from keeping that limit, not from simply having more.

author: Seneca
text: When I say that I do nothing for the sake of pleasure, I allude to that wise man, whom alone you admit to be capable of pleasure: now I do not call a man wise who is overcome by anything, let alone by pleasure: yet, if engrossed by pleasure, how will he resist toil, danger, want, and all the ills which surround and threaten the life of man?
plain: If comfort is running the whole evening, hard tasks, awkward conversations, and tight months will all feel impossible. Pleasure makes a poor boss for a real working week.

author: Seneca
text: The pleasures of wise men, on the other hand, are mild, decorous, verging on dullness, kept under restraint and scarcely noticeable, and are neither invited to come nor received with honour when they come of their own accord, nor are they welcomed with any delight by those whom they visit, who mix them up with their lives and fill up empty spaces with them, like an amusing farce in the intervals of serious business.
plain: The pleasures that sit well in a life are quiet ones, fitted around real work and family, not the loud treats you chase and then talk about all night.

author: Seneca
text: I myself believe, though my Stoic comrades would be unwilling to hear me say so, that the teaching of Epicurus was upright and holy, and even, if you examine it narrowly, stern: for this much talked of pleasure is reduced to a very narrow compass, and he bids pleasure submit to the same law which we bid virtue do⁠—I mean, to obey nature.
plain: A modest pleasure, kept inside what your body and your ordinary week can actually carry, is a very different thing from grabbing whatever feels good late at night.

author: Seneca
text: Let virtue lead the way and bear the standard: we shall have pleasure for all that, but we shall be her masters and controllers; she may win some concessions from us, but will not force us to do anything.
plain: Let good sense walk in front. You can still enjoy a meal, a laugh, or a quiet evening, as long as those pleasures ask rather than drag you.

author: Seneca
text: Even the joy which arises from virtue, although it be a good thing, yet is not a part of absolute good, any more than cheerfulness or peace of mind, which are indeed good things, but which merely follow the highest good, and do not contribute to its perfection, although they are generated by the noblest causes.
plain: A calm mood and a light feeling are welcome side effects, but they follow from living decently. Chasing the feeling itself, on a Friday night, misses the real point.

author: Seneca
text: True happiness, therefore, consists in virtue: and what will this virtue bid you do?
plain: A good life shows up in what you actually do on a normal weekday: how you speak to people, how you spend the evening, and what you quietly refuse.

author: Seneca
text: Why do you pay regard to common rumour, and feel annoyed by calumnious gossip? why is your estate more elaborately kept than its natural use requires? why do you not dine according to your own maxims? why is your furniture smarter than it need be? why do you drink wine that is older than yourself? why are your grounds laid out?
plain: Gossip should not set your mood tonight, and a house, a wardrobe, or a drink cupboard need not be fancier than the life you actually live with your family.

author: Seneca
text: You argue about the life and death of another, and yelp at the name of men whom some peculiarly noble quality has rendered great, just as tiny curs do at the approach of strangers: for it is to your interest that no one should appear to be good, as if virtue in another were a reproach to all your crimes.
plain: Sniping at people who live a bit more cleanly often protects your own excuses. Their example feels like an attack only if your evenings cannot bear the comparison.

author: Seneca
text: Let us therefore inquire, not what is most commonly done, but what is best for us to do, and what will establish us in the possession of undying happiness, not what is approved of by the vulgar, the worst possible exponents of truth.
plain: Ask what would actually make your weeks feel solid, not what the group chat is doing on Saturday night. Popular habits are a weak guide to a good life.

author: Seneca
text: Men deserve praise for engaging in profitable studies, even though they stop short of producing any results.
plain: Starting a useful bit of learning still counts, even if work and family mean you do not finish the course this year. The effort itself is already worthwhile.

author: Seneca
text: Why does he say that wealth ought to be despised and yet possess it? that life should be despised, and yet live? that health should be despised, and yet guard it with the utmost care, and wish it to be as good as possible?
plain: You can hold money, health, and ordinary home comfort lightly, and still look after them with real care. Using those things well is different from worshipping them every day.

author: Seneca
text: Who can doubt, however, that the wise man, if he is rich, has a wider field for the development of his powers than if he is poor, seeing that in the latter case the only virtue which he can display is that of neither being perverted nor crushed by his poverty, whereas if he has riches, he will have a wide field for the exhibition of temperance, generosity, laboriousness, methodical arrangement, and grandeur.
plain: Having a bit more money gives you more ways to be fair, generous, and organised at home. Having less still lets you stay decent, just on a narrower stage.

author: Seneca
text: Cease, then, forbidding philosophers to possess money: no one has condemned wisdom to poverty.
plain: Being thoughtful about life does not require an empty bank account. You can earn, save for the family, and still keep your head about what the money is for.

author: Seneca
text: He who believes giving to be an easy matter, is mistaken: it offers very great difficulties, if we bestow our bounty rationally, and do not scatter it impulsively and at random.
plain: Handing money or time to other people is harder than it looks, once you pause and choose carefully instead of giving on a whim in the group chat.

author: Seneca
text: Learn, then, since we both agree that they are desirable, what my reason is amongst counting them among good things, and in what respects I should behave differently to you if I possessed them.
plain: Nice things can be welcome in a home without being what makes a life good. If they arrived tomorrow, your manners with family should stay much the same.

author: Seneca
text: You accustom yourself to them and cling to them as if somebody had promised that they should be yours forever, but a wise man never thinks so much about poverty as when he is surrounded by riches.
plain: It is easy to treat a good salary and a full fridge as permanent. The steadier habit is to remember, while you have them, how quickly they can go.

author: Seneca
text: Praise good men, if you are able: if not, pass them by in silence: if indeed you take pleasure in this offensive abusiveness, fall foul of one another: for when you rave against Heaven, I do not say that you commit sacrilege, but you waste your time.
plain: If you can speak well of decent people, do it. If you cannot, stay quiet, because sneering at them all evening only burns time you could have used.

author: Seneca
text: Let us seek for some blessing, which does not merely look fine, but is sound and good throughout alike, and most beautiful in the parts which are least seen: let us unearth this.
plain: Look for a kind of wellbeing that still holds in the bits nobody posts: how you are at home late, and how you treat people when there is no audience.

author: Seneca
text: Our highest good may also be defined otherwise; that is to say, the same idea may be expressed in different language.
plain: There are several plain ways to describe what a good life is, and they point to the same thing: a steady mind showing up in ordinary working days.

author: Seneca
text: With them you may class men whose dull nature and want of self-knowledge reduces them to the level of cattle, mere animals: there is no difference between the one and the other, because the latter have no reason, while the former have only a corrupted form of it, crooked and cunning to their own hurt.
plain: Drifting through the week without noticing your own evening habits is a kind of sleepwalking. Clever excuses that harm you are worse than having no plan at all.

author: Seneca
text: The happy man, therefore, is he who can make a right judgment in all things: he is happy who in his present circumstances, whatever they may be, is satisfied and on friendly terms with the conditions of his life.
plain: You are in a good place when you judge situations fairly and can be on decent terms with the life you actually have this month, work, home, and all.

author: Seneca
text: Even those very people who declare the highest good to be in the belly, see what a dishonourable position they have assigned to it: and therefore they say that pleasure cannot be parted from virtue, and that no one can either live honourably without living cheerfully, nor yet live cheerfully without living honourably.
plain: Parking the whole point of life in your stomach or your glass leaves it in a poor spot. Feeling cheerful and living decently need each other, but neither is just appetite.

author: Seneca
text: What answer are we to make to the reflection that pleasure belongs to good and bad men alike, and that bad men take as much delight in their shame as good men in noble things?
plain: A good time is not proof of a good choice, because people enjoy harmful habits just as warmly as others enjoy doing the decent thing on a quiet night.

author: Seneca
text: For this cause reason will never call to its aid blind and fierce impulses, over whom she herself possesses no authority, and which she never can restrain save by setting against them similar and equally powerful passions, as for example, fear against anger, anger against sloth, greed against timidity.
plain: Clear thinking does not borrow blind rage to get a hard job done, because a feeling you cannot steer will not stay useful once the argument at home really starts.

author: Seneca
text: What, indeed, is it except anger, so ruinous to itself, that overthrows barbarians, who have so much more bodily strength than we, and are so much better able to endure fatigue?
plain: Rage is strong enough to wreck even tough people. The person who explodes at work or at home is often the one who comes off worst in the end.

author: Seneca
text: Why do you fear that filial piety will not prove a sufficient spur to him even without anger?
plain: Care for your family does not need a hot temper to keep it moving. Duty, affection, and a clear head are already enough reason to show up for them.

author: Seneca
text: Moreover, qualities which we ought to possess become better and more desirable the more extensive they are: if justice is a good thing, no one will say that it would be better if any part were subtracted from it; if bravery is a good thing, no one would wish it to be in any way curtailed: consequently the greater anger is, the better it is, for whoever objected to a good thing being increased?
plain: If losing your temper were a real strength, more of it would make the household better, and nobody who has lived with shouting believes that for a minute.

author: Seneca
text: It is impossible, says Theophrastus, for a good man not to be angry with bad men.
plain: Some people hold that a decent person must bristle at every bad deed around them, as if staying calm around poor behaviour were the same as agreeing with it.

author: Seneca
text: The sinner ought, therefore, to be corrected both by warning and by force, both by gentle and harsh means, and may be made a better man both towards himself and others by chastisement, but not by anger: for who is angry with the patient whose wounds he is tending?
plain: You can correct someone firmly, at home or at work, the way a nurse deals with a wound, without adding rage to the help you are already giving.

author: Seneca
text: We do not, therefore, need an angry chastiser to punish the erring and wicked: for since anger is a crime of the mind, it is not right that sins should be punished by sin.
plain: Putting someone right at home does not require you to be in a fury. Meeting a fault with another fault, your own temper, only adds a second mess to the evening.

author: Seneca
text: These arms, which Aristotle assigns to virtue, fight of their own accord, do not wait to be seized by the hand, and possess a man instead of being possessed by him.
plain: Once temper takes the lead in a disagreement, it uses you. You stop choosing your words, and the row in the kitchen starts choosing them for you instead.

author: Seneca
text: Irascibility, I say, has this fault⁠—it is loath to be ruled: it is angry with the truth itself, if it comes to light against its will: it assails those whom it has marked for its victims with shouting and riotous noise and gesticulation of the entire body, together with reproaches and curses.
plain: A hot temper hates being told to wait even a minute. It shouts over the facts, waves its arms, and turns a simple correction at work into a public scene.

author: Seneca
text: Neither ought it to be believed that anger contributes anything to magnanimity: what it gives is not magnanimity but vain glory.
plain: Blowing up can feel like strength or personal pride, but it is mostly a performance. Real steadiness does not need an audience to see you win the argument.

author: Seneca
text: There is therefore nothing great or noble in anger, even when it seems to be powerful and to contemn both gods and men alike.
plain: Fury can look grand when someone towers over a meeting room, yet there is nothing fine in it, only noise that colleagues and family will remember later on.

author: Seneca
text: In the next place, no one is so low in station as not to be able to hope to inflict punishment even upon the greatest of men: we all are powerful for mischief.
plain: Almost anyone can cause real harm, whatever their job title. A sharp message, a long sulk, or a rumour is enough to wound someone who seemed out of reach.

author: Seneca
text: What anger is has been sufficiently explained. The difference between it and irascibility is evident: it is the same as that between a drunken man and a drunkard; between a frightened man and a coward.
plain: One angry evening is not the same as a character built on anger, just as one night of drinking is not the same as being ruled by drink.

author: Seneca
text: We have now finished our enquiry as to what anger is, whether it exists in any other creature besides man, what the difference is between it and irascibility, and how many forms it possesses. Let us now enquire whether anger be in accordance with nature, and whether it be useful and worth entertaining in some measure.
plain: Once you have felt a flare of temper, check whether any of that heat is actually helping the conversation, the shift, or the evening waiting for you at home.

author: Seneca
text: We char crooked spearshafts to straighten them, and force them by driving in wedges, not in order to break them, but to take the bends out of them; and, in like manner, by applying pain to the body or mind we correct dispositions which have been rendered crooked by vice.
plain: A bent habit sometimes needs pressure to straighten, the way heat and effort reshape a warped piece of wood, and the aim is repair, not snapping the person.

author: Seneca
text: May it not be that, although anger be not natural, it may be right to adopt it, because it often proves useful?
plain: People defend a temper by saying it gets results at work. It is worth asking whether the same job could be done without the collateral damage at home.

author: Seneca
text: My first book, Novatus, had a more abundant subject: for carriages roll easily down hill: now we must proceed to drier matters.
plain: Describing a problem out loud is the easy downhill part. The drier work is changing the habit, on ordinary evenings when nobody is applauding the effort at all.

author: Seneca
text: You will rather think that we should not be angry with people’s faults; for what shall we say of one who is angry with those who stumble in the dark, or with deaf people who cannot hear his orders, or with children, because they forget their duty and interest themselves in the games and silly jokes of their companions?
plain: Getting cross with someone who cannot properly hear you, or with a child lost in play, misses the point. Plenty of adult mistakes at home deserve that same slack.

author: Seneca
text: If, again, it is without strength, it is much more exposed to contempt, and cannot avoid ridicule: for what is more flat than anger when it breaks out into meaningless ravings?
plain: A temper that cannot actually change anything just looks silly. Ranting in the kitchen or in a voice note, with no power behind it, only invites a wince.

author: Seneca
text: He may be protected against the inclement time of the year by dwelling in a favoured spot, or he may have so trained his body to endurance that it feels neither heat nor cold.
plain: You can arrange your evenings so fewer things set you off, or you can train yourself until small irritations, heat, delay, and noise, do not land quite so hard.

author: Seneca
text: There is no reason why we should seek to defend such a passion as this or excuse its excesses by declaring it to be either useful or unavoidable.
plain: There is no need to call a kitchen blow-up useful or inevitable. You can admit it was too much without building a neat theory that protects the next one.

author: Seneca
text: Anger, then, must never become a habit with us, but we may sometimes affect to be angry when we wish to rouse up the dull minds of those whom we address, just as we rouse up horses who are slow at starting with goads and firebrands.
plain: Do not let real anger become your everyday manner at home. A firm tone, used on purpose to wake someone up, is a tool you can put down afterwards.

author: Seneca
text: In like manner, dispositions which are naturally bold produce irritability, and, being hot and fiery, have no mean or trivial qualities, but their energy is misdirected, as happens with all those who without training come to the front by their natural advantages alone, whose minds, unless they be brought under control, degenerate from a courageous temper into habits of rashness and reckless daring.
plain: Natural drive is a real gift until it has no training behind it. Then confidence turns into snapping at people, and courage slides into reckless rows you later regret.

author: Seneca
text: Those animals, urges our opponent, are held to be the most generous who have large capacity for anger.
plain: People sometimes admire a fierce temper in a friend, as if the sharpest person in the room were also the bravest. Heat and real generosity are not the same quality.

author: Seneca
text: A man ought to be neither robber nor victim, neither tenderhearted nor cruel. The former belongs to an over-weak mind, the latter to an over-hard one.
plain: You do not have to choose between being a doormat and being a bully. Kindness without a spine, and hardness without care, both make home and work worse.

author: Seneca
text: Now that we have discussed the questions propounded concerning anger, let us pass on to the consideration of its remedies.
plain: Understanding why you flare up at home is only the opening. The part that changes a week is what you practise the next time your voice starts to rise.

author: Seneca
text: A hot mind is naturally the most prone to anger: for as there are four elements, consisting of fire, air, earth, and water, so there are powers corresponding and equivalent to each of these, namely, hot, cold, dry, and moist.
plain: Some people run naturally hot and reach anger faster, the way some rooms overheat in summer. Knowing your own temperature is part of handling a tense evening well.

author: Seneca
text: Whither, say you, does this inquiry tend? That we may know what anger is: for if it springs up against our will, it never will yield to reason: because all the motions which take place without our volition are beyond our control and unavoidable, such as shivering when cold water is poured over us, or shrinking when we are touched in certain places.
plain: A first jolt of irritation can arrive like a shiver, before you choose it. What you do in the next minute is the part that still belongs to you.

author: Seneca
text: But just as nature makes some men prone to anger, so there are many other causes which have the same power as nature.
plain: A quick temper is not only something you were born with. Short sleep, drink, stress, and the company you keep can push you just as hard towards a row.

author: Seneca
text: It is, I assure you, of the greatest service to boys that they should be soundly brought up, yet to regulate their education is difficult, because it is our duty to be careful neither to cherish a habit of anger in them, nor to blunt the edge of their spirit.
plain: Raising children well means keeping their spirit alive without training them to explode, because a house that runs too sharp soon turns anger into the everyday family habit.

author: Seneca
text: These precepts, however, apply to our children: in ourselves the accident of birth and our education no longer admits of either mistakes or advice; we must deal with what follows.
plain: Childhood lessons arrive a bit too late for grown adults. What you can still shape is the next habit, starting with how tonight usually goes in your own house.

author: Seneca
text: Everyone knows the story of the tyrannicide who, being caught before he had accomplished his task, and being tortured by Hippias to make him betray his accomplices, named the friends of the tyrant who stood around, and everyone to whom he knew the tyrant’s safety was especially dear.
plain: Under real pressure, a clever person can refuse to betray the people who matter, even while seeming to give an answer. Courage is sometimes quiet and precise, not loud.

author: Seneca
text: Readiness to believe what we hear causes very great mischief; we ought often not even to listen, because in some cases it is better to be deceived than to suspect deceit.
plain: Believing every sharp story you hear starts a lot of needless rows. Sometimes it is kinder, and safer for everyone, not to chase a rumour about a friend all evening.

author: Seneca
text: Another consequence of this will be, that we shall not be exasperated by the slightest and most contemptible trifles.
plain: A delayed reply, a messy kitchen, or a tone in a text does not have to wreck the night. Small irritations can stay small if you let them.

author: Seneca
text: We are angry, either with those who can, or with those who cannot do us an injury.
plain: Notice who you are actually cross with. Some people can hurt your job or your home, and some cannot, and the second kind do not deserve the same heat.

author: Seneca
text: There are some things which are unable to hurt us, and whose power is exclusively beneficial and salutary, as, for example, the immortal gods, who neither wish nor are able to do harm: for their temperament is naturally gentle and tranquil, and no more likely to wrong others than to wrong themselves.
plain: Some forces in a day are not out to get you, and raging at them is wasted breath. Save your energy for what a person can actually change tonight.

author: Seneca
text: If we desire to be impartial judges of all that takes place, we must first convince ourselves of this, that no one of us is faultless: for it is from this that most of our indignation proceeds.
plain: Most hot indignation shrinks once you honestly remember your own faults. It is hard to stay lofty about a colleague's mistake when your own week was hardly spotless.

author: Seneca
text: The greatest remedy for anger is delay: beg anger to grant you this at the first, not in order that it may pardon the offence, but that it may form a right judgment about it:⁠—if it delays, it will come to an end.
plain: The best move with anger is to wait. Give the feeling a little time and it often fades before you send the text or raise your voice at home.

author: Seneca
text: None of these things which casually influence the mind deserve to be called passions: the mind, if I may so express it, rather suffers passions to act upon itself than forms them.
plain: A flicker of annoyance when the phone buzzes is not yet a full temper, and you can let it pass through without building it into a row at home.

author: Seneca
text: Some offences we ourselves witness: in these cases let us examine the disposition and purpose of the offender.
plain: When you see the offence yourself, look at what the person meant, not only at how it landed. Purpose changes what a fair response at work should be.

author: Seneca
text: There are, as I have stated, two cases which produce anger: first, when we appear to have received an injury, about which enough has been said, and, secondly, when we appear to have been treated unjustly: this must now be discussed.
plain: Anger usually starts from one of two feelings: that someone hurt you, or that they treated you unfairly. Naming which one it is can calm the next conversation.

author: Seneca
text: In the latter case it is a shame to be conquered; in the former it is a shame to conquer.
plain: Losing a quiet contest of kindness is the embarrassing outcome. Winning a contest of payback, the last word or the colder silence, is the result to regret at home.

author: Seneca
text: The wrongs of the powerful must not only be borne, but borne with a cheerful countenance: they will repeat the wrong if they think they have inflicted it.
plain: When someone with power over your job is unfair, wearing the hurt on your face often invites a repeat. A steady expression gives them less to feed on.

author: Seneca
text: We must, therefore, refrain from anger, whether he who provokes us be on a level with ourselves, or above us, or below us.
plain: A hot temper is a poor reply whether the person is your boss, your equal, or someone who answers to you at work. Rank never makes that heat useful.

author: Seneca
text: Does anyone wish to strike his enemy so hard, as to leave his own hand in the wound, and not to be able to recover his balance after the blow? yet such a weapon is anger: it is scarcely possible to draw it back.
plain: Lashing out is like a blow you cannot pull back. The words stay in the other person, and you are still off balance when the evening should have moved on.

author: Seneca
text: Furthermore, that you may know in what manner passions begin and swell and gain spirit, learn that the first emotion is involuntary, and is, as it were, a preparation for a passion, and a threatening of one.
plain: The first flash is involuntary, a warning rather than the whole storm. What swells afterwards is where a text, a tone, or a drink can make it grow.

author: Seneca
