text: We must also enquire whether those whose cruelty knows no bounds, and who delight in shedding human blood, are angry when they kill people from whom they have received no injury, and who they themselves do not think have done them any injury; such as were Apollodorus or Phalaris.
plain: Cruelty can enjoy itself without any real injury to avenge. That is a useful warning that harshness, even in small digs at people, can slowly become a taste.

author: Seneca
text: To rejoice and be glad is the proper and natural function of virtue: it is as much beneath her dignity to be angry, as to mourn: now, sorrow is the companion of anger, and all anger ends in sorrow, either from remorse or from failure.
plain: A decent life has more room for gladness than for rage. Anger tends to finish in regret, either because you went too far or because the outburst failed.

author: Seneca
text: What, too, can be more unworthy of the wise man, than that his passions should depend upon the wickedness of others?
plain: Your mood does not have to be rented out to other people's bad behaviour. If their faults set the tone of your whole evening, they are effectively holding the remote.

author: Seneca
text: Why need I dwell upon individual cases? Be assured, when you see the forum crowded with a multitude, the Saepta swarming with people, or the great Circus, in which the greater part of the people find room to show themselves at once, that among them there are as many vices as there are men.
plain: Any busy train, pub, or office holds as many flaws as it holds people. Expecting a crowd to be pure is a fast route to a sour mood.

author: Seneca
text: The wise man will never cease to be angry, if he once begins, so full is every place of vices and crimes.
plain: If you start being angry at every fault you notice around you, you will never stop, because a normal day at work and at home is full of small ones.

author: Seneca
text: We will now, my Novatus, attempt to do that which you so especially long to do, that is, to drive out anger from our minds, or at all events to curb it and restrain its impulses.
plain: You may not erase temper from your character completely, and you do not have to. Curbing the impulse, so it does not run the evening, is already a real change.

author: Seneca
text: That which is diseased can never bear to be handled without complaining: it is best, therefore, to apply remedies to oneself as soon as we feel that anything is wrong, to allow oneself as little licence as possible in speech, and to restrain one’s impetuosity: now it is easy to detect the first growth of our passions: the symptoms precede the disorder.
plain: A sore mood complains at the lightest touch, so catch it while it is small. Fewer sharp words, and a pause when you feel the rush, can stop the evening turning.

author: Seneca
text: It is better not to see or to hear everything: many causes of offence may pass by us, most of which are disregarded by the man who ignores them.
plain: You do not have to read every comment or replay every slight. A lot of offence dies on its own when you refuse to pick it up on your phone.

author: Seneca
text: A large part of mankind manufacture their own grievances either by entertaining unfounded suspicions or by exaggerating trifles.
plain: A lot of personal grievances are home-made, built from a suspicion with thin evidence or from a tiny slight blown up over the course of a long evening.

author: Seneca
text: Fight hard with yourself, and if you cannot conquer anger, do not let it conquer you: you have begun to get the better of it if it does not show itself, if it is not given vent.
plain: Wrestle the temper inwardly if you must. Even if it is still there, you have started to win when it gets no speech, no text, and no scene.

author: Seneca
text: King Cambyses was excessively addicted to wine. Præxaspes was the only one of his closest friends who advised him to drink more sparingly, pointing out how shameful a thing drunkenness was in a king, upon whom all eyes and ears were fixed.
plain: Heavy drinking is especially costly when people are watching you lead, at work or at home, because the shame spreads much further than the night itself ever reaches.

author: Seneca
text: I have no doubt that Harpagus must have given some such advice to the king of the Persians and of himself, in anger at which the king placed Harpagus’s own children before him on the dinner-table for him to eat, and asked him from time to time, whether he liked the seasoning.
plain: When power and rage mix, advice can be punished in hideous ways. That old story is a warning about what temper does once nobody can tell a person to stop.

author: Seneca
text: Would to heaven that such savagery had contented itself with foreign examples, and that barbarity in anger and punishment had not been imported with other outlandish vices into our Roman manners!
plain: It is tempting to think a brutal temper belongs only to other people and far-off places. It arrives in ordinary homes the moment we start to copy what we have seen.

author: Seneca
text: It is to the purpose that we should know how haughtily his cruelty was exercised, although someone might suppose that we are wandering from the subject and embarking on a digression; but this digression is itself connected with unusual outbursts of anger.
plain: Looking hard at famous public outbursts is not gossip for its own sake. It shows how pride and temper can inflate a small slight into something much uglier.

author: Seneca
text: Thus, the king of the Persians cut off the noses of a whole nation in Syria, wherefore the place is called Rhinocolura.
plain: Rage in charge of a crowd can punish everyone at once, and the damage gets a name that outlasts the ruler. Group blame is still a modern habit.

author: Seneca
text: This man was angry with an unknown and inoffensive nation, which nevertheless was able to feel his wrath; but Cyrus was angry with a river.
plain: Temper can pick a fight with people who never harmed you, or even with a traffic jam and a slow laptop. The target does not have to deserve it.

author: Seneca
text: These should be regarded as examples to be avoided, and what I am about to relate, on the contrary, to be followed, being examples of gentle and lenient conduct in men who both had reasons for anger and power to avenge themselves.
plain: Some stories are warnings, and some are models. The useful ones show people who had both a reason to rage and the power to punish, and still stayed measured.

author: Seneca
text: Have I more authority in my own house than the Emperor Augustus possessed throughout the world? yet he was satisfied with leaving the society of his maligner.
plain: If a powerful person can simply leave the company of someone who slanders them, you can step out of a row at home without needing the last word.

author: Seneca
text: As it is a consolation to a humble man in trouble that the greatest are subject to reverses of fortune, and a man weeps more calmly over his dead son in the corner of his hovel if he sees a piteous funeral proceed out of the palace as well; so one bears injury or insult more calmly if one remembers that no power is so great as to be above the reach of harm.
plain: It steadies you to remember that status does not shield anyone. A boss, a celebrity, or a confident friend can be hurt too, so the insult is less personal.

author: Seneca
text: Besides, what you intend to do is to endure both injury and anger. Why do you bear with the delirium of a sick man, or the ravings of a madman, or the impudent blows of a child?
plain: You already cope with a child's flailing and with someone who is not themselves. An insult from a worked-up adult can be met with that same steady patience.

author: Seneca
text: How far better is it to heal an injury than to avenge it? Revenge takes up much time, and throws itself in the way of many injuries while it is smarting under one.
plain: Mending a hurt takes less out of a week than paying it back. Revenge keeps you in the fight and collects fresh injuries while you are still sore.

author: Seneca
text: It is shameful to hate him whom you praise: but how much more shameful is it to hate a man for something for which he deserves to be pitied?
plain: It is odd to praise someone in public and resent them in private. It is worse to hate them for a weakness that actually calls for a bit of pity.

author: Seneca
text: It is therefore essential to prove its unseemliness and ferocity, and to place distinctly before our eyes how monstrous a thing it is that one man should rage against another, with what frantic violence he rushes to destroy alike himself and his foe, and overthrows those very things whose fall he himself must share.
plain: Two people tearing into each other often wreck the very home, job, or friendship they both still need afterwards. The mess lands on the angry person as well.

author: Seneca
text: How much better is it to observe how trifling, how inoffensive are the first beginnings of anger?
plain: The start of anger is usually tiny: a look, a delay, a clumsy sentence. Seeing how small it is at the beginning makes it easier to leave there.

author: Seneca
text: No man is satisfied with his own lot if he fixes his attention on that of another: and this leads to our being angry even with the gods, because somebody precedes us, though we forget of how many we take precedence, and that when a man envies few people, he must be followed in the background by a huge crowd of people who envy him.
plain: Staring at someone else's life, on a phone or across the office, makes your own lot feel thin. You forget how many people would gladly trade places with you tonight.

author: Seneca
text: Let different qualities in different people keep us from quarrelling with them: let us fear to be angry with some, feel ashamed of being angry with others, and disdain to be angry with others.
plain: Different people call for different brakes on a quarrel. With some you hold back out of respect, with others out of embarrassment, and with some because it is beneath you.

author: Seneca
text: Come now, let us enumerate the other causes of anger: they are food, drink, and the showy apparatus connected with them, words, insults, disrespectful movements of the body, suspicions, obstinate cattle, lazy slaves, and spiteful construction put upon other men’s words, so that even the gift of language to mankind becomes reckoned among the wrongs of nature.
plain: Rows are often lit by drink, a showy meal, a rude gesture, or a suspicious reading of someone's words. The spark is frequently smaller than the scene that follows.

author: Seneca
text: You are indignant at being answered back by your slave, your freedman, your wife, or your client: and then you complain of the State having lost the freedom which you have destroyed in your own house: then again if he is silent when you question him, you call it sullen obstinacy.
plain: Some people demand a reply and then hate the reply, or hate the silence. You cannot preach fairness at work and shut conversation down in your own kitchen.

author: Seneca
text: All our senses should be educated into strength: they are naturally able to endure much, provided that the spirit forbears to spoil them.
plain: Your nerves can handle more noise, waiting, and ordinary discomfort than you first think, if your mind stops telling you that every small irritation is a full emergency.

author: Seneca
text: At the dinner-table some jokes and sayings intended to give you pain have been directed against you: avoid feasting with low people.
plain: If supper with certain friends always includes a joke at your expense, choose different company. You do not have to sit there and call it a good night.

author: Seneca
text: Someone has offered you an insult? Not a greater one, probably, than was offered to the Stoic philosopher Diogenes, in whose face an insolent young man spat just when he was lecturing upon anger.
plain: An insult, even a gross one in public, is smaller than the story you may build around it. People have stayed calm with far worse landing on them.

author: Seneca
text: We have now succeeded, my Novatus, in properly regulating our own minds: they either do not feel anger or are above it: let us next see how we may soothe the wrath of others, for we do not only wish to be whole, but to heal.
plain: Once your own temper is a bit steadier, the next skill is calming someone else in the room. Looking after a friendship includes helping the other person come down as well.

author: Seneca
text: There may be some doubt about the others, but at any rate no passion has a worse look.
plain: Whatever you think about other strong feelings in a crisis, anger still has the worst face. People remember the expression long after they forget the point you were making.

author: Seneca
text: I myself, by Hercules, am scandalized at your treatment and am grieved beyond measure, but we must wait for a proper opportunity.
plain: You can agree that something was out of order and still ask everyone to wait for a better moment. Sympathy and delay can sit in the same conversation.

author: Seneca
text: Let us be free from this evil, let us clear our minds of it, and extirpate root and branch a passion which grows again wherever the smallest particle of it finds a resting-place.
plain: Leave no little pocket of temper tucked away to grow back later. A sulk you keep just in case is enough seed for the same row to return next week.

author: Seneca
text: Instead of acting thus, why do you not rather draw together what there is of your short life, and keep it peaceful for others and for yourself? why do you not rather make yourself beloved by everyone while you live, and regretted by everyone when you die?
plain: Life is already short enough without spending the evenings on old grudges. Use the time to be someone your family is glad to have around, and would honestly miss.

author: Seneca
text: You ask me, whither does all this tend? To prove, I answer, that no one should imagine himself to be safe from anger, seeing that it rouses up even those who are naturally gentle and quiet to commit savage and violent acts.
plain: Do not assume a gentle nature makes you safe in a crisis. Quiet people can still be pushed into a harsh act when temper finally finds a way out.

author: Seneca
text: There is no greater proof of magnanimity than that nothing which befalls you should be able to move you to anger.
plain: A strong mind shows itself when bad news, a snub, or a messy day fails to tip you into anger. That calm is a bigger achievement than winning the row.

author: Seneca
text: Be assured that the same rule applies both to public and private life: simple and manageable undertakings proceed according to the pleasure of the person in charge of them, but enormous ones, beyond his capacity to manage, are not easily undertaken.
plain: Small and clear tasks go where you steer them. Huge plans launched in a temper, grand paybacks and dramatic exits, are usually more than one tired evening can carry.

author: Seneca
text: Since we know not how to endure an injury, let us take care not to receive one: we should live with the quietest and easiest-tempered persons, not with anxious or with sullen ones: for our own habits are copied from those with whom we associate, and just as some bodily diseases are communicated by touch, so also the mind transfers its vices to its neighbours.
plain: If slights are hard for you to carry, spend time with calm people rather than anxious or sullen ones. Moods spread through a household the way a cold does.

author: Seneca
text: Irascible men ought not to meddle with the more serious class of occupations, or, at any rate, ought to stop short of weariness in the pursuit of them; their mind ought not to be engaged upon hard subjects, but handed over to pleasing arts: let it be softened by reading poetry, and interested by legendary history: let it be treated with luxury and refinement.
plain: If you run hot, do not grind at the heaviest tasks until you are frayed. A walk, a book, or music in the evening can soften the edge before it cuts someone.

author: Seneca
text: … why do they with great unanimity recommend vices to us? even though we attempt nothing else that would do us good, yet retirement in itself will be beneficial to us: we shall be better men when taken singly⁠—and if so, what an advantage it will be to retire into the society of the best of men, and to choose some example by which we may guide our lives!
plain: Stepping back from a noisy crowd can already make you better, especially if you then keep company, even through books, with people whose lives you would actually copy.

author: Seneca
text: Now I will prove to you that I am not deserting the tenets of the Stoics: for they themselves have not deserted them: and yet I should be able to plead a very good excuse even if I did follow, not their precepts, but their examples.
plain: Following the lived example of steady people can be as loyal to a good tradition as repeating its rules. What they did on hard days is the real guide.

author: Seneca
text: I will show that this is approved of by the Stoics also, not that I have laid any commandment upon myself to do nothing contrary to the teaching of Zeno and Chrysippus, but because the matter itself allows me to follow the precepts of those men; for if one always follows the precepts of one man, one ceases to be a debater and becomes a partisan.
plain: You can agree with a sound tradition without swearing loyalty to one famous teacher. Copying a single person turns you into a fan, when you could still be thinking for yourself.

author: Seneca
text: This may be that of the Athenians or Carthaginians, or of any other city which does not belong to all men but to some especial ones.
plain: Your loyalty is not only to one town, one workplace, or one familiar group chat. There is a wider circle of people you still owe ordinary fairness to each day.

author: Seneca
text: We have a habit of saying that the highest good is to live according to nature: now nature has produced us for both purposes, for contemplation and for action.
plain: A human life needs both quiet reflection and practical doing. Thinking things through in the evening, then getting on with the work next morning, belongs in the same week.

author: Seneca
text: It is by no means desirable that one should merely strive to accumulate property without any love of virtue, or do nothing but hard work without any cultivation of the intellect, for these things ought to be combined and blended together; and, similarly, virtue placed in leisure without action is but an incomplete and feeble good thing, because she never displays what she has learned.
plain: Money without character, and endless grind without any real thought, both come out thin. What you learn in a quiet hour only finishes when it shows up in how you act.

author: Seneca
text: Moreover, there are three kinds of life, and it is a stock question which of the three is the best: the first is devoted to pleasure, the second to contemplation, the third to action.
plain: People roughly organise a life around enjoyment, around thinking, or around getting things done. A whole week that is only pleasure, or only rush, leaves something important out.

author: Seneca
text: Add to this that, according to the doctrine of Chrysippus, a man may live at leisure: I do not say that he ought to endure leisure, but that he ought to choose it.
plain: Time off is not only something you put up with when work pauses. You can choose a quieter stretch on purpose, and treat it as part of a brave life.

author: Seneca
text: These remarks of mine apply only to imperfect, commonplace, and unsound natures, not to the wise man, who needs not to walk with timid and cautious gait: for he has such confidence in himself that he does not hesitate to go directly in the teeth of Fortune, and never will give way to her.
plain: Most of us still need caution with risk, money, and big moods. Full confidence that never flinches is a rare height, not the standard for a normal Tuesday.

author: Seneca
text: I will set sail unless anything happens to prevent me, I shall be praetor, if nothing hinders me, my financial operations will succeed, unless anything goes wrong with them.
plain: Make the plan, and quietly allow that something may block it. That small reserve keeps a cancelled trip or a delayed promotion from feeling like a personal failure.

author: Seneca
text: Yet we gain nothing by getting rid of all personal causes of sadness, for sometimes we are possessed by hatred of the human race.
plain: Sorting out your own private sorrows is not the whole job. Some gloom is just a general sourness towards people, and that one follows you into every room you enter.

author: Seneca
text: I have now, my beloved Serenus, given you an account of what things can preserve peace of mind, what things can restore it to us, what can arrest the vices which secretly undermine it: yet be assured, that none of these is strong enough to enable us to retain so fleeting a blessing, unless we watch over our vacillating mind with intense and unremitting care.
plain: Advice about calm only works if you keep an eye on your mood all week. A wavering mind needs steady attention, not a single good resolution on Monday.

author: Seneca
text: but what does he gain by so doing if he does not escape from himself? he follows himself and weighs himself down by his own most burdensome companionship.
plain: Changing city, job, or the usual pub does very little if you bring the same restless mind with you. You cannot leave yourself behind in the last place.

author: Seneca
text: You ask me what I think we had better make use of to help us to support this ennui.
plain: That bored, itchy restlessness in the evening needs something sturdier than another long scroll on your phone. A real task or a real conversation carries the mood much better.

author: Seneca
text: To me, my dearest Serenus, Athenodorus seems to have yielded too completely to the times, to have fled too soon: I will not deny that sometimes one must retire, but one ought to retire slowly, at a foot’s pace, without losing one’s ensigns or one’s honour as a soldier: those who make terms with arms in their hands are more respected by their enemies and more safe in their hands.
plain: Leaving a bad situation is sometimes right, but do it slowly and with your self-respect intact. A rushed exit can cost more honour than the stress you were escaping.

author: Seneca
text: Could you anywhere find a miserable city than that of Athens when it was being torn to pieces by the thirty tyrants? they slew thirteen hundred citizens, all the best men, and did not leave off because they had done so, but their cruelty became stimulated by exercise.
plain: Harshness grows when it is practised, and a workplace or a household can turn grim surprisingly fast once that tone becomes the daily drill for the people in charge.

author: Seneca
text: We ought, however, first to examine our own selves, next the business which we propose to transact, next those for whose sake or in whose company we transact it.
plain: Before you give a big yes, check three plain things: your own limits, the task itself, and the people you would be doing it with or for all year.

author: Seneca
text: In all cases one should be careful in one’s choice of men, and see whether they be worthy of our bestowing a part of our life upon them, or whether we shall waste our own time and theirs also: for some even consider us to be in their debt because of our services to them.
plain: Choose carefully who gets a slice of your weeks. Some people will treat your help as a debt you still owe, and both of you will waste the time.

author: Seneca
text: Let us now pass on to the consideration of property, that most fertile source of human sorrows: for if you compare all the other ills from which we suffer⁠—deaths, sicknesses, fears, regrets, endurance of pains and labours⁠—with those miseries which our money inflicts upon us, the latter will far outweigh all the others.
plain: Money worries outlast a surprising number of other troubles. The fear of losing it, and the fuss of guarding it, can crowd a home more than people admit.

author: Seneca
text: We shall be pleased with this measure of wealth if we have previously taken pleasure in thrift, without which no riches are sufficient, and with which none are insufficient, especially as the remedy is always at hand, and poverty itself by calling in the aid of thrift can convert itself into riches.
plain: Enough feels like enough once you have enjoyed living simply, because without that habit no pay rise settles you, and with it a modest week already covers what matters.

author: Seneca
text: You have asked me, Lucilius, why, if the world be ruled by providence, so many evils befall good men?
plain: Decent people still meet illness, redundancy, and family pain, and the old question remains how a life can be hard on them without the whole thing being meaningless.

author: Seneca
text: Why do many things turn out badly for good men? Why, no evil can befall a good man; contraries cannot combine.
plain: A hard week can hit a decent person, yet the claim is that it does not make them bad, and it does not reach the part of them that chooses.

author: Seneca
text: Of all these propositions that which I have stated first appears the most difficult to prove, I mean, that the things which we dread and shudder at are to the advantage of those to whom they happen.
plain: The strange suggestion here is that some events you dread, a loss, a setback, a frightening week, can still leave you more capable than you were the month before.

author: Seneca
text: You are a great man; but how am I to know it, if fortune gives you no opportunity of showing your virtue?
plain: Character often stays hidden until something difficult finally asks for it. A calm week at work does not display the steadiness that a real family setback would show.

author: Seneca
text: Add to this that it is to the advantage of everyone that the best men should, so to speak, be on active service and perform labours: God has the same purpose as the wise man, that is, to prove that the things which the herd covets and dreads are neither good nor bad in themselves.
plain: When capable people meet hard work and still stay decent, it shows the rest of us that status and disaster are not the real measure of a life.

author: Seneca
text: He protects and saves them. Does anyone besides this demand that God should look after the baggage of good men also?
plain: What is worth guarding in a crisis is the person, not every possession and plan travelling with them. The luggage can be lost and the life still hold.

author: Seneca
source: On the Firmness of the Wise Person, chapter 1
text: I might truly say, Serenus, that there is as wide a difference between the Stoics and the other sects of philosophers as there is between men and women, since each class contributes an equal share to human society, but the one is born to command, the other to obey.
plain: One way of living tries to steer, and another keeps getting steered by moods and fashion. The firmer way is the one that gives orders to your own impulses.

author: Seneca
source: On the Firmness of the Wise Person, chapter 10
text: Since we have now discussed the first part of our subject, let us pass on to the second, in which we will prove by arguments, some of which are our own, but which for the most part are Stoic commonplaces, that the wise man cannot be insulted.
plain: A settled mind can hear a slight and not be truly wounded by it. The insult reaches the ears, and it does not have to reach the person underneath.

author: Seneca
source: On the Firmness of the Wise Person, chapter 11
text: Besides this, as most insults proceed from those who are haughty and arrogant and bear their prosperity ill, he has something wherewith to repel this haughty passion, namely, that noblest of all the virtues, magnanimity, which passes over everything of that kind as like unreal apparitions in dreams and visions of the night, which have nothing in them substantial or true.
plain: Plenty of casual insults come from people puffed up by a good run. You can let those remarks pass like a dream that looked solid and was not.

author: Seneca
source: On the Firmness of the Wise Person, chapter 12
text: In the same spirit in which we deal with boys, the wise man deals with all those whose childhood still endures after their youth is past and their hair is grey.
plain: Some adults still act like children, grey hair or not. You can answer them with the patience you would use for a stroppy teenager, and skip the feud.

author: Seneca
source: On the Firmness of the Wise Person, chapter 13
text: What, then, is there to prevent your believing this strength of mind to belong to the wise man, when you can see the same thing existing in others, though not from the same cause?⁠—for what physician is angry with a crazy patient? who takes to heart the curses of a fever-stricken one who is denied cold water?
plain: A nurse does not take a sick person's insults to heart. You can use that same distance when someone's pain or temper is talking, not their settled judgement.

author: Seneca
source: On the Firmness of the Wise Person, chapter 14
text: Such madness possesses some men that they imagine it possible for an affront to be put upon them by a woman.
plain: It is a shaky kind of pride that feels specially wounded because of who delivered the slight. A remark is not heavier because it came from someone you look down on.

author: Seneca
source: On the Firmness of the Wise Person, chapter 15
text: It is from your own weakness that you form your idea of his colossal mind, and when you have thought how much you yourselves could endure to suffer, you place the limit of the wise man’s endurance a little way beyond that.
plain: We guess other people's strength from our own limits, then add a little. Real steadiness may sit much further on than the most we can picture on a bad day.

author: Seneca
source: On the Firmness of the Wise Person, chapter 16
text: Now if even Epicurus, who made more concessions to the body than anyone, takes a spirited tone with regard to injuries, what can appear beyond belief or beyond the scope of human nature amongst us Stoics?
plain: Even people who allow the body plenty of ordinary comfort can still refuse to be crushed by a public insult. Holding your ground is not some superhuman party trick.

author: Seneca
source: On the Firmness of the Wise Person, chapter 17
text: Chrysippus says that a man was enraged because someone called him a sea-sheep; we have seen Fidus Cornelius, the son-in-law of Ovidius Naso, weeping in the Senate-house because Corbulo called him a plucked ostrich; his command of his countenance did not fail him at other abusive charges, which damaged his character and way of life; at this ridiculous saying he burst into tears.
plain: People sometimes stay perfectly calm under a serious accusation, then fall apart at a silly nickname. The joke hurts more only because pride was already waiting for it.

author: Seneca
source: On the Firmness of the Wise Person, chapter 19
text: We ought not to engage in quarrels and wrangling; we ought to betake ourselves far away and to disregard everything of this kind which thoughtless people do (indeed thoughtless people alone do it), and to set equal value upon the honours and the reproaches of the mob; we ought not to be hurt by the one or to be pleased by the other.
plain: Step away from wrangling. Treat a pile of online praise and a pile of online scorn as the same cheap noise, and do not let either one steer your evening.

author: Seneca
source: On the Firmness of the Wise Person, chapter 3
text: It has not been my object to decorate the wise man with mere imaginary verbal honours, but to raise him to a position where no injury will be permitted to reach him.
plain: The aim is not a fancy title for being unbothered. It is a place in yourself where a slight, at work or online, is not allowed to land as a wound.

author: Seneca
source: On the Firmness of the Wise Person, chapter 4
text: Even when powerful men, raised to positions of high authority, and strong in the obedience of their dependents, strive to injure him, all their darts fall as far short of his wisdom as those which are shot upwards by bowstrings or catapults, which, although they rise so high as to pass out of sight, yet fall back again without reaching the heavens.
plain: People with rank can aim hard at you, and still miss the part that matters. A lot of workplace hostility climbs high and drops back without touching your judgement.

author: Seneca
source: On the Firmness of the Wise Person, chapter 5
text: If you think fit, my Serenus, let us distinguish between injury and insult. The former is naturally the more grievous, the latter less important, and grievous only to the thin-skinned, since it angers men but does not wound them.
plain: A real practical loss and a rude remark are very different weights. The remark mostly angers people who are already thin-skinned, and it does not have to cut.

author: Seneca
source: On the Firmness of the Wise Person, chapter 6
text: Consider now, whether any thief, or false accuser, or headstrong neighbour, or rich man enjoying the power conferred by a childless old age, could do any injury to this man, from whom neither war nor an enemy whose profession was the noble art of battering city walls could take away anything.
plain: If a full-blown crisis cannot take your character away from you, then a rude neighbour, a false story, or a wealthy local bully is unlikely to manage it either.

author: Seneca
source: On the Firmness of the Wise Person, chapter 7
text: A man may become mischievous, and yet do no actual mischief: if a man lies with his own wife as if she were a stranger, he will commit adultery, but his wife will not; if a man gives me poison and the poison lose its strength when mixed with food, that man, by administering the poison, has made himself a criminal, even though he has done no hurt.
plain: Someone can dirty their own character with a bad intention even when no harm actually lands. The stain stays on the person who meant it, not on everyone nearby.

author: Seneca
source: On the Firmness of the Wise Person, chapter 8
text: Moreover, justice can suffer nothing unjust, because contraries cannot coexist; but an injury can only be done unjustly, therefore an injury cannot be done to the wise man.
plain: A truly fair mind is not a place where injustice can settle and stay. People may try to wrong you, and the attempt need not become an injury inside you.

author: Seneca
source: On the Firmness of the Wise Person, chapter 9
text: He therefore endures everything in the same spirit with which he endures the cold of winter and the severities of climate, fevers, diseases, and other chance accidents, nor does he entertain so high an opinion of any man as to suppose that he acts of set purpose, which belongs to the wise man alone.
plain: Treat an ordinary human slight the way you treat bad weather or a bout of illness. It happens, and it is rarely a clever plot designed around your evening.

author: Seneca
source: On the Shortness of Life, chapter 10
text: If I chose to divide this proposition into separate steps, supported by evidence, many things occur to me by which I could prove that the lives of busy men are the shortest of all.
plain: A packed diary can make a whole life feel strangely short, because the days are spent reacting, and very little of them is actually lived with any purpose.

author: Seneca
source: On the Shortness of Life, chapter 12
text: Some men’s leisure is busy: in their country house or on their couch, in complete solitude, even though they have retired from all men’s society, they still continue to worry themselves: we ought not to say that such men’s life is one of leisure, but their very business is sloth.
plain: Time off that is spent fretting on the sofa is not rest. Worry can be a full-time job, even in a quiet house with the phone face down.

author: Seneca
source: On the Shortness of Life, chapter 14
text: The only persons who are really at leisure are those who devote themselves to philosophy: and they alone really live: for they do not merely enjoy their own lifetime, but they annex every century to their own: all the years which have passed before them belong to them.
plain: The people who seem most alive are the ones who use quiet hours to think, so that other people's hard-won years become part of how they live now.

author: Seneca
source: On the Shortness of Life, chapter 15
text: None of these men will force you to die, but all of them will teach you how to die: none of these will waste your time, but will add his own to it.
plain: Good examples will not steal your years. They show you how to meet an ending, and the attention you give them comes back as extra life, not less.

author: Seneca
source: On the Shortness of Life, chapter 16
text: Those men lead the shortest and unhappiest lives who forget the past, neglect the present, and dread the future: when they reach the end of it the poor wretches learn too late that they were busied all the while that they were doing nothing.
plain: The most drained weeks are the ones where yesterday is ignored, today is skipped, and tomorrow is only a worry. Constant busyness can be a clever way of doing nothing.

author: Seneca
source: On the Shortness of Life, chapter 18
text: Wherefore, my dearest Paulinus, tear yourself away from the common herd, and since you have seen more rough weather than one would think from your age, betake yourself at length to a more peaceful haven: reflect what waves you have sailed through, what storms you have endured in private life, and brought upon yourself in public.
plain: If your years have already been stormy, at work and in private, you are allowed to head for quieter water instead of staying in the crowd out of habit.

author: Seneca
source: On the Shortness of Life, chapter 2
text: Why do we complain of Nature? she has dealt kindly with us. Life is long enough, if you know how to use it.
plain: There is no need to blame the years for being short. Most people have time enough, and they spend it on things they will not remember next month.

author: Seneca
source: On the Shortness of Life, chapter 20
text: When, therefore, you see a man often wear the purple robes of office, and hear his name often repeated in the forum, do not envy him: he gains these things by losing so much of his life.
plain: The person whose name keeps coming up, at work or online, may be paying for that attention with hours they no longer really own. Sheer envy misses the real invoice.

author: Seneca
source: On the Shortness of Life, chapter 4
text: You will find that the most powerful and highly-placed men let fall phrases in which they long for leisure, praise it, and prefer it to all the blessings which they enjoy.
plain: Listen to busy, successful people talk and you will hear them praise a free afternoon more warmly than the perks they are known for. They already feel the shortage.

author: Seneca
source: On the Shortness of Life, chapter 9
text: Can anything be mentioned which is more insane than the ideas of leisure of those people who boast of their worldly wisdom?
plain: Nothing is odder than the holidays planned by people who pride themselves on being practical, yet fill the break with the same rush they claim to have escaped.

author: Zeno of Citium
source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of the Philosophers, Book 7, Life of Zeno, section 19
text: He was once asked how he felt when people abused him, and he said, “As an ambassador feels when he is sent away without an answer.”
plain: When someone lays into you and you do not fire back, you are like a messenger who delivers the point and leaves without a reply. Silence can be the whole answer.

author: Zeno of Citium
source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of the Philosophers, Book 7, Life of Zeno, section 19
text: On one occasion, when he saw a slave belonging to one of his friends severely bruised, he said to his friend, “I see the footsteps of your anger.”
plain: Bruises, slammed doors, and a frightened kitchen all show where a temper has walked. Other people can see that trail even when you think the row stayed private.

author: Zeno of Citium
source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of the Philosophers, Book 7, Life of Zeno, section 19
text: A young man was talking a great deal of nonsense, and he said to him, “This is the reason why we have two ears and only one mouth, that we may hear more and speak less.”
plain: You have a bias built in for listening. In a meeting or a family talk, hearing more and speaking less will save you from a lot of nonsense.

author: Zeno of Citium
source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of the Philosophers, Book 7, Life of Zeno, section 19
text: When he was asked what a friend was, he replied, “Another I.”
plain: A real friend is a second self: someone whose good day and bad day you can feel almost as your own, without losing where you stop and they start.

author: Zeno of Citium
source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of the Philosophers, Book 7, Life of Zeno, section 19
text: Apollonius of Tyre tells us, that when Crates dragged him by the cloak away from Stilpo, he said, “O Crates, the proper way to take hold of philosophers is by the ears; so now do you convince me and drag me by them; but if you use force towards me, my body may be with you, but my mind with Stilpo.”
plain: You change someone's mind by giving them reasons they can hear, not by dragging them along. Their body can follow you while their judgement stays where it was.

author: Zeno of Citium
source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of the Philosophers, Book 7, Life of Zeno, section 19
text: One of his sayings used to be, that vanity was the most unbecoming of all things, and especially so in the young.
plain: Showing off sits badly on almost anyone, and it sits even worse on someone young who is still learning the job, the friendship, or how to spend an evening.

author: Zeno of Citium
source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of the Philosophers, Book 7, Life of Zeno, section 5
text: Others say, that while he was staying at Athens he heard of a shipwreck, and said, “Fortune does well in having driven us on philosophy.”
plain: A sudden loss that shuts one comfortable road can push you towards a more serious life. Wrecked plans sometimes drop you somewhere more useful than the original destination.

author: Zeno of Citium
source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of the Philosophers, Book 7, Life of Zeno, section 5
text: So that it is related that he said, “I now find that I made a prosperous voyage when I was wrecked.”
plain: Looking back from a calmer year, the setback that felt like a total wreck can turn out to have been the trip that actually got you somewhere worth reaching.

author: Plato
text: There you are mistaken: a man who is good for anything ought not to calculate the chance of living or dying; he ought only to consider whether in doing anything he is doing right or wrong—acting the part of a good man or of a bad.
plain: A useful person does not spend the decision weighing survival against failure. The only question that matters is whether the act is right, and whether it fits a decent life.

author: Plato
text: You, my friend,—a citizen of the great and mighty and wise city of Athens,—are you not ashamed of heaping up the greatest amount of money and honour and reputation, and caring so little about wisdom and truth and the greatest improvement of the soul, which you never regard or heed at all?
plain: Chasing money, status, and a famous name while ignoring truth and the care of your inner life is something to be ashamed of, even in a celebrated city.

author: Plato
text: For if you kill me you will not easily find a successor to me, who, if I may use such a ludicrous figure of speech, am a sort of gadfly, given to the state by God; and the state is a great and noble steed who is tardy in his motions owing to his very size, and requires to be stirred into life. I am that gadfly which God has attached to the state, and all day long and in all places am always fastening upon you, arousing and persuading and reproaching you.
plain: A huge, sleepy community needs a persistent sting that wakes it, argues with it, and will not let comfort win. That irritating voice is a gift, not a nuisance to swat.

author: Plato
text: he must look to himself, and seek virtue and wisdom before he looks to his private interests, and look to the state before he looks to the interests of the state; and that this should be the order which he observes in all his actions.
plain: Look after your own character, and put virtue and wisdom ahead of private gain. Care for the community itself before you chase what the community can give you.

author: Plato
text: and if I say again that daily to discourse about virtue, and of those other things about which you hear me examining myself and others, is the greatest good of man, and that the unexamined life is not worth living, you are still less likely to believe me.
plain: Talking every day about virtue, and testing your own life and other people, is held up as the greatest human good. A life that never faces that test is not worth keeping.

author: Plato
text: I will withdraw them, rather than admit that a man can be temperate or wise who does not know himself; and I am not ashamed to confess that I was in error. For self-knowledge would certainly be maintained by me to be the very essence of knowledge, and in this I agree with him who dedicated the inscription, 'Know thyself!' at Delphi.
plain: The speaker would rather drop an earlier claim than say a person can be wise without knowing himself. He treats the Delphi line, know yourself, as the heart of real knowledge.

author: Plato
text: In questions of just and unjust, fair and foul, good and evil, which are the subjects of our present consultation, ought we to follow the opinion of the many and to fear them; or the opinion of the one man who has understanding?
plain: On questions of right and wrong, the crowd is a poor guide. Follow the person who actually understands, and protect the part of you that justice can strengthen.

author: Plato
text: And I should like to know whether I may say the same of another proposition--that not life, but a good life, is to be chiefly valued?
plain: Staying alive is not the prize. What deserves your loyalty is a life that is decent, fair, and able to stand up when you look at it closely.

author: Plato
text: Tell me, then, whether you agree with and assent to my first principle, that neither injury nor retaliation nor warding off evil by evil is ever right.
plain: Do not answer a wrong with another wrong, and do not treat hitting back as a form of defence. That refusal is the starting rule for any honest argument about how to live.

author: Plato
text: Then these are the points at issue between us—are they not? I was saying that to do is worse than to suffer injustice?
plain: The argument worth having is this: committing an injustice does more damage than suffering one. Agree or disagree, but do not slide past that claim.

author: Plato
text: NICIAS: I mean to say, Laches, that courage is the knowledge of that which inspires fear or confidence in war, or in anything.
plain: One definition on the table says courage is knowing what should scare you and what should steady you, in battle and in ordinary life. The dialogue then tests whether that knowledge is enough.

author: Plato
text: The inference at which we arrive for the third or fourth time is, that education is the constraining and directing of youth towards that right reason, which the law affirms, and which the experience of the eldest and best has agreed to be truly right.
plain: Education, on this account, steers the young toward the reason the law and the most experienced people have agreed is genuinely right. It is direction, not a pile of loose opinions.

author: Plato
text: And let the figure be composite--a pair of winged horses and a charioteer. Now the winged horses and the charioteers of the gods are all of them noble and of noble descent, but those of other races are mixed; the human charioteer drives his in a pair; and one of them is noble and of noble breed, and the other is ignoble and of ignoble breed; and the driving of them of necessity gives a great deal of trouble to him.
plain: Picture the soul as a driver with two horses, one steady and one unruly. Keeping both on the road takes constant effort, and that struggle is the daily work of character.

author: Plato
text: The divine is beauty, wisdom, goodness, and the like; and by these the wing of the soul is nourished, and grows apace; but when fed upon evil and foulness and the opposite of good, wastes and falls away.
plain: What you feed grows. Beauty, wisdom, and goodness strengthen the part of you that lifts, while foul habits starve it until it can no longer rise.

author: Plato
text: The chariots of the gods in even poise, obeying the rein, glide rapidly; but the others labour, for the vicious steed goes heavily, weighing down the charioteer to the earth when his steed has not been thoroughly trained:--and this is the hour of agony and extremest conflict for the soul.
plain: A trained team moves smoothly under the rein. An untrained, vicious pull drags the driver down, and that clash is the hardest hour the soul has to face.

author: Plato
text: The right-hand horse is upright and cleanly made; he has a lofty neck and an aquiline nose; his colour is white, and his eyes dark; he is a lover of honour and modesty and temperance, and the follower of true glory; he needs no touch of the whip, but is guided by word and admonition only.
plain: The better impulse stands tall, loves honour, modesty, and balance, and answers a word of guidance. It does not need force, only a clear reminder of what is worthy.

author: Plato
text: And when this has happened several times and the villain has ceased from his wanton way, he is tamed and humbled, and follows the will of the charioteer, and when he sees the beautiful one he is ready to die of fear.
plain: Repeated correction wears down the wild impulse until it stops lunging and accepts the driver. Fear of slipping back becomes a guard, and the soul stays close to what it loves.

author: Plato
text: Then, I said, no man voluntarily pursues evil, or that which he thinks to be evil. To prefer evil to good is not in human nature; and when a man is compelled to choose one of two evils, no one will choose the greater when he may have the less.
plain: Nobody walks toward what they truly believe is bad if a better path is open. When both options are poor, a person still reaches for the smaller harm.

author: Plato
text: You know also that the beginning is the most important part of any work, especially in the case of a young and tender thing; for that is the time at which the character is being formed and the desired impression is more readily taken.
plain: The opening of any work leaves the deepest mark, and that is especially true while someone is still young and soft. Character takes its shape in those early impressions.

author: Plato
text: And would you not say that he is temperate who has these same elements in friendly harmony, in whom the one ruling principle of reason, and the two subject ones of spirit and desire are equally agreed that reason ought to rule, and do not rebel?
plain: Temperance is the inner agreement that reason should lead, while spirit and appetite stay willing partners and do not rise up against that lead. Harmony, not suppression, is the point.

author: Plato
text: And now, I said, let me show in a figure how far our nature is enlightened or unenlightened:—Behold! human beings living in a underground den, which has a mouth open towards the light and reaching all along the den; here they have been from their childhood, and have their legs and necks chained so that they cannot move, and can only see before them, being prevented by the chains from turning round their heads.
plain: Imagine people who have sat in a cave since childhood, fixed so they can see only the wall in front of them. What they take for the whole world is only the shadow of it.

author: Plato
text: In the next place, he will regulate his bodily habit and training, and so far will he be from yielding to brutal and irrational pleasures, that he will regard even health as quite a secondary matter; his first object will be not that he may be fair or strong or well, unless he is likely thereby to gain temperance, but he will always desire so to attemper the body as to preserve the harmony of the soul?
plain: A healthy or handsome body is a side issue. The aim is to train the body so the soul stays in tune, and to refuse fitness that costs that inner balance.

author: Plato
text: And in the acquisition of wealth there is a principle of order and harmony which he will also observe; he will not allow himself to be dazzled by the foolish applause of the world, and heap up riches to his own infinite harm?
plain: Money has its own order. Take what you need without being dazzled by applause, and refuse a pile of riches that would wreck the life you are trying to keep steady.

author: Plato
text: 'He is a great spirit (daimon), and like all spirits he is intermediate between the divine and the mortal.' 'And what,' I said, 'is his power?' 'He interprets,' she replied, 'between gods and men, conveying and taking across to the gods the prayers and sacrifices of men, and to men the commands and replies of the gods; he is the mediator who spans the chasm which divides them
plain: Love, in this telling, stands between gods and mortals and carries messages both ways. It is the link that joins what would otherwise stay cut off from each other.

author: Plato
text: SOCRATES: I see, my dear Theaetetus, that Theodorus had a true insight into your nature when he said that you were a philosopher, for wonder is the feeling of a philosopher, and philosophy begins in wonder.
plain: Wonder is where thinking starts. If a puzzle makes your head swim, that confusion is not a failure but the feeling that shows a mind has begun to wake.
